title: Buying a Used Van: What the MOT History Tells You That the Advert Does Not
desc: How to read a van MOT history before you buy: the mileage trail, the advisories that actually matter on a working van, the gaps sellers never mention, and what a free check cannot tell you.
body:
The short version
  • A van that has done 90,000 honest miles is usually a better buy than one showing 45,000 with a patchy MOT trail.
  • Vans wear differently to cars. Look for suspension, brakes and corrosion advisories, not engine faults.
  • Most vans need their first MOT at three years, the same as a car. Vehicles used to carry passengers for hire or reward are the exception.
  • A gap in the MOT record is the single biggest thing an advert will never mention. It usually means the van sat unused or was off the road being repaired.
  • Every check on this page is free and takes about two minutes with the registration.

Why an MOT trail says more about a van than a car

A used car is mostly bought by one person who drove it to work. A used van has usually been a tool, and tools get used hard. That changes what you should be looking for in the record.

Vans carry weight. Weight destroys suspension, brakes and tyres long before it troubles an engine. So when you read a van MOT history, the interesting failures are almost never dramatic. They are the same boring components appearing again and again, which tells you the vehicle has spent its life loaded.

The other difference is mileage. A van doing 25,000 miles a year on motorways is in better mechanical shape than one doing 8,000 miles a year of stop-start urban delivery work, even though the second one looks better in the advert. Motorway miles are gentle. Multi-drop miles are not.

You can see all of this for free. Put the registration into the MOT history checker and read the trail rather than the headline.

Read the mileage trail first, before anything else

Every MOT records the odometer reading. Lined up in order, those readings are a chart of how the van has actually been used, and they are very hard to fake because they were recorded by different testers at different garages on different dates.

Three things to look for:

What you seeWhat it usually means
Steady 15,000 to 30,000 miles a yearNormal working van. Nothing to worry about.
A year with almost no milesThe van sat. Ask why. Long standing is hard on brakes, tyres, seals and batteries.
A reading lower than the one before itStop. Either a clerical error at the garage or the odometer has been wound back. Ask the seller to explain it in writing before you go any further.
A large jump then a sudden drop to very low annual mileageOften a change of use, for example a courier van sold on to a private owner. Not a problem in itself, but the hard miles are already in the vehicle.

Clocking is a real and profitable crime, and vans are a favourite target because high mileage hits van values hard. Our guide on how to spot a clocked vehicle goes through the full method, and it applies identically to vans.

The advisories that matter on a van

An advisory is the tester telling you something is wearing but has not yet failed. On a van, a repeated advisory is more useful than a one-off failure, because it shows a pattern the seller has ignored.

  • Corrosion, especially underneath. The most expensive words in a van MOT history. Look for corrosion noted on the subframe, sills, suspension mounting points or brake pipes. Once corrosion is structural, the repair bill can exceed the value of the van.
  • Suspension and springs. Repeated advisories here mean the van has been run loaded, often overloaded. Expect more of the same.
  • Brake pipes and hoses. Cheap to fix now, an MOT failure later, and a safety issue in between.
  • Play in steering or wheel bearings. Normal wear on a working van, but note how often it recurs.
  • Oil leaks noted as slight. Watch whether the same leak is still slight three years later or has been upgraded to a failure.

What matters far less than people think: a bulb, a wiper blade, a number plate lamp, or a single tyre below the limit. Those are consumables and they tell you nothing about the vehicle.

If you want the full breakdown of what actually causes failures and roughly what each one costs to put right, read what actually fails an MOT in the UK.

Gaps in the record, and what they hide

This is the check almost nobody does, and it is the one that finds the problems.

Lay the test dates out in order. An MOT lasts twelve months, so the tests should be roughly a year apart. If there is a gap of eighteen months, two years or more, the van was not being used on the road during that time. That is not automatically bad, but there are only a few explanations:

  1. It was declared off the road because the owner did not need it. Common with seasonal trades and second vans.
  2. It was being repaired after an accident or a major mechanical failure.
  3. It failed and was left until someone decided whether it was worth fixing.
  4. It was in a compound after being written off, then repaired and put back on the road.

Numbers three and four are the ones you care about. A free MOT history will not tell you which of the four it was. It will tell you that a gap exists, so you can ask the seller a specific question instead of a general one. "Why is there no MOT between March 2023 and October 2024" is a much better question than "has it had any accidents".

The free checks to run before you view

All of these take a registration number and no money.

CheckWhat it tells youWhere
MOT history and mileage trailUse, condition pattern, gaps, clocking riskOur free checker
Tax status and MOT expiryWhether it is road legal todayGOV.UK vehicle enquiry
Clean air zone and ULEZ liabilityWhether it costs you a daily charge to drive into a cityOur ULEZ checker
RecallsOutstanding safety recalls not yet carried outGOV.UK vehicle recalls

ULEZ matters more for vans than for cars. A pre-Euro 6 diesel van is charged daily in London and in a growing number of clean air zones, and for a working vehicle that can be hundreds of pounds a month. Check it before you buy, not after. You can compare two vehicles side by side if you are choosing between them.

What a free check cannot tell you

Be clear about the limits, because plenty of sites blur them.

A free MOT history check shows tests, mileage, failures and advisories. It does not show outstanding finance, whether the vehicle has been written off by an insurer, whether it is recorded as stolen, or whether it has been scrapped or exported. Those come from finance houses, the insurance industry register and the police, and no free service has them.

For a cheap van bought privately, an MOT history plus a careful inspection covers most of the risk. For anything expensive, or anything bought from a stranger with a story, a paid vehicle history check is worth the money. That is a genuine gap in what we currently offer for free, and we would rather say so than pretend otherwise.

The verdict

Read the mileage trail, count the gaps, and look for the same advisory repeating. A van with high miles, a complete record and boring consumable advisories is a better buy than a low mileage van with a two year hole in its history and fresh paint underneath. The record is free, it is official, and the seller cannot edit it.

title: What an MOT Actually Costs in 2026, and When the Retest Is Free
desc: The legal maximum MOT fee is 54.85 pounds for a car and 29.65 for a motorcycle, unchanged since 2010. What garages really charge, the free retest rules, and five ways to pay less.
body:
The short version
  • The legal maximum for a car MOT is £54.85. It has not changed since April 2010.
  • Motorcycles are capped at £29.65. Most garages charge well under both caps.
  • Typical real-world price is £30 to £45 for a car, and promotional deals from about £20.
  • From 6 July 2026 the caps rose for heavy vehicles: £70 for HGVs, £50 for trailers, £90 for buses and coaches.
  • A retest is often free. Whether it is depends entirely on where the vehicle went after it failed.

The legal maximum, and why nobody charges it

DVSA sets a maximum MOT fee by vehicle class. A garage may charge less. It may not charge more.

VehicleMaximum fee
Car, up to 8 passenger seats (class 4)£54.85
Motorcycle over 200cc (class 4 motorcycle)£29.65
Motorcycle up to 200cc£29.65 or less depending on class
Goods vehicle up to 3,000kg (class 7)£58.60
HGV, from 6 July 2026£70.00
Trailer, from 6 July 2026£50.00
Bus or coach, from 6 July 2026£90.00

Caps as published by DVSA and current in August 2026. The car and motorcycle figures have been frozen since April 2010.

Here is the part that matters. Almost no garage charges the cap. The MOT itself is barely profitable at any price; garages want the repair work that follows. So the test is used as a loss leader, and a typical honest price in 2026 is somewhere between £30 and £45. Chains and fast-fit centres run £20 to £25 offers regularly.

If you are quoted £54.85, you are being charged the absolute maximum by a garage that has decided you will not shop around. Ring two more.

When a retest is free, and when it is not

This is the rule that costs people the most money because it is not obvious and nobody explains it at the counter.

  • Leave the vehicle at the test centre and have the repair done there. If it is retested before the end of the next working day, the retest is normally free.
  • Take the vehicle away and bring it back within 10 working days. You get a partial retest, free for a specified list of items. This covers most common failures.
  • Bring it back after 10 working days, or with a failure outside the partial list, and you pay for a full test again.

So the expensive mistake is failing on a Friday, leaving the car on the drive for three weeks, then paying twice. If you cannot fix it quickly, at least get it back inside the ten working days.

Ask the question before you hand over the keys: "if it fails and I repair it myself, is the retest free within ten working days?" A garage that hesitates is telling you something.

Five ways to pay less, and one to ignore

  1. Book at a council test centre if you have one nearby. Some local authority sites test but do not repair, so they have no incentive to find work. This removes the conflict of interest entirely.
  2. Ask for MOT only, no service. Bundled deals often hide a service you did not need.
  3. Book in the quiet months. March and September are the busiest because of plate changes, and prices firm up. January and February are quiet.
  4. Fix the obvious things yourself first. Bulbs, wipers, screenwash, tyre pressures and a number plate light. Lighting is the single biggest failure category in Great Britain and most of it is a bulb.
  5. Test early. You can test up to a month minus a day before expiry and keep the original expiry date, which gives you time to fix a failure without the car being off the road illegally.

What to ignore: pre-MOT checks sold as a separate paid service by the same garage doing the MOT. You are paying twice to be told the same thing.

The cost that is not the test

The test fee is the small number. The repairs are the big one, and the MOT history tells you what is coming before you pay for anything.

Put the registration into our free MOT history checker and read the advisories from the last two tests. An advisory is the tester saying a component is wearing but has not failed yet. The same advisory appearing twice is a failure being scheduled for you.

Our guide on what actually fails an MOT goes through the categories and rough repair costs, and the defect categories explains the difference between dangerous, major and minor.

Driving without one

Driving without a valid MOT can bring a fine of up to £1,000. If the vehicle is in a dangerous condition it rises to up to £2,500, three penalty points and a possible disqualification. Your insurance may also be affected.

There are two legal exceptions: driving to a pre-booked MOT test, and driving to a garage for repairs needed for the test. Both need to be genuine, and "I was on my way to book one" is not one of them.

Full detail in the MOT rules and fines guide.

The verdict

The cap is £54.85 for a car and £29.65 for a bike, and you should almost never pay it. Ring three garages, ask about the free retest window before you book, fix the bulbs yourself, and spend the difference on the advisories the last test already warned you about.

title: Every UK Clean Air Zone in 2026: Who Pays, How Much, and Where Cars Are Exempt
desc: Seven charging zones in England plus London ULEZ. Only three charge private cars. The full table, the Euro standards that decide it, and why Scotland works completely differently.
body:
The short version
  • England has seven charging clean air zones in 2026: Birmingham, Bath, Bristol, Bradford, Portsmouth, Sheffield and Tyneside, plus London ULEZ separately.
  • Only Birmingham, Bristol and London charge private cars. In Bath, Bradford, Portsmouth and Tyneside a compliant or non-compliant car pays nothing.
  • Vans and taxis are charged in far more places than cars are. If you drive a diesel van, this matters to you and not to your neighbour with the same age car.
  • Scotland works differently: Glasgow, Edinburgh, Aberdeen and Dundee operate bans with penalty charges, not daily fees.
  • The test is almost always Euro 6 for diesel, Euro 4 for petrol. Check your own vehicle free on our ULEZ and clean air zone checker.

Every charging zone in England, and who pays

Clean air zones come in classes, and the class decides which vehicles are charged. That is why two cities can both have a zone and only one of them charges you.

ZoneClassCars charged?Typical daily charge
BirminghamDYes£8 cars, taxis, private hire and vans. £50 HGVs, coaches and buses.
BristolDYesAll non-compliant vehicle types charged.
BathCNoCars and motorcycles exempt. Vans, taxis, minibuses, coaches, buses and HGVs charged.
BradfordCNoPrivate cars exempt. Most other vehicles charged.
SheffieldCNoCars exempt. Taxis, vans and buses charged.
Tyneside (Newcastle and Gateshead)CNoCars exempt. Most commercial vehicles charged.
PortsmouthBNoOnly non-compliant taxis, buses, coaches and HGVs. Cars and light goods vehicles not charged.

Positions as at August 2026. Zones are set by individual councils and can change, so confirm with the council before travelling if the charge would be significant.

London is separate and stricter. ULEZ covers all London boroughs and charges non-compliant cars, vans and motorcycles daily. The Congestion Charge is a different scheme again, in a smaller central area, and you can be liable for both on the same day.

What actually makes a vehicle compliant

The threshold is the emissions standard, not the age on the logbook, though age is a good proxy.

FuelStandard neededRoughly means
Petrol car or vanEuro 4Registered from about January 2006
Diesel car or vanEuro 6Registered from about September 2015
MotorcycleEuro 3Registered from about July 2007
Electric or hydrogenExemptAny age

Two things people get wrong. First, a diesel is judged far more harshly than a petrol, so a 2014 diesel is non-compliant while a 2007 petrol is fine. Second, these are guides, not guarantees. A vehicle registered close to the cut-off may or may not meet the standard depending on the exact engine. Check the registration rather than assuming.

Vehicles over 40 years old are generally exempt as historic vehicles, and there are local exemptions and discounts in most zones for residents, blue badge holders and some commercial operators. Those are set locally and you have to apply.

Scotland is a ban, not a charge

This catches people out badly, because the money involved is much larger.

Glasgow, Edinburgh, Aberdeen and Dundee run low emission zones. A non-compliant vehicle is not charged a daily fee. It is prohibited from entering, and if it does, a penalty charge applies. The penalty starts at a set amount and doubles for each repeat offence within a period, up to a capped maximum.

So an English driver who is used to paying £8 and thinking nothing of it can take a diesel into Glasgow and get a penalty instead. There is no "pay to enter" option. Check before you drive north.

Why this hits vans hardest

Look back at the table. In four of the seven English zones a private car pays nothing while a van pays. That is deliberate: commercial vehicles do more miles in city centres and older diesel vans are among the dirtiest things on the road.

For a working van this stops being a curiosity and becomes a real operating cost. A tradesperson driving into Birmingham five days a week in a pre-2015 diesel van is looking at roughly £40 a week, about £2,000 a year, purely to keep working the same patch.

That number should change what you buy. Our guide on buying a used van covers the rest of the checks, but on emissions the rule is simple: for a diesel van used in cities, Euro 6 is not a nice-to-have.

How to check yours in about a minute

  1. Put the registration into our free ULEZ and clean air zone checker. It tells you the likely compliance position from the vehicle record.
  2. If it is borderline, confirm with the operator of the specific zone. Every zone has its own official checker and theirs is the one that decides.
  3. If you are buying, check before you buy. A non-compliant diesel is cheaper for a reason, and that reason will be charged to you daily.
  4. Check the MOT history at the same time. It costs nothing and it is the other half of the same decision.

The verdict

If you drive a petrol car from 2006 or later, or any diesel from late 2015, you are almost certainly fine everywhere in England. If you drive a diesel van, you are the vehicle these schemes were designed around and you should check every city you work in. And if you are heading to Scotland, remember that there is no daily charge to pay, only a penalty to avoid.

title: Category A, B, S and N Explained: What a Written-Off Car Really Means
desc: A write-off is an insurance decision, not a mechanical verdict. What each category means, which can never be driven again, what it does to value and insurance, and how to find out.
body:
The short version
  • A write-off is an insurance decision, not a mechanical verdict. Plenty of written-off cars are structurally fine.
  • Category A and B can never legally return to the road. If someone is selling you one as a runner, walk away and report it.
  • Category S means structural damage was repaired. Category N means non-structural. Both can be sold and driven legally.
  • Expect a Cat S or N car to be worth roughly 20% to 40% less than the same car with clean history, and expect some insurers to decline it.
  • A free MOT history will not tell you a vehicle was written off. That data comes from the insurance industry register and needs a paid check.

What a write-off actually is

When a vehicle is damaged, the insurer compares the repair cost against the vehicle value. If repairing it does not make commercial sense, they write it off, pay the owner and take ownership of the wreck.

That is an economic judgement about one vehicle at one moment. A ten year old car with £2,500 of damage is written off. The same damage to a two year old car is repaired. So "written off" tells you the repair was uneconomic for the insurer, not that the car is unsafe.

Where it becomes your problem is that the wreck is then sold at salvage, repaired by someone, and put back on the market. Sometimes that is done properly. Sometimes it is not.

The four categories

CategoryWhat it meansCan it be driven again?
AScrap only. The entire vehicle must be crushed, including every part.Never. Nothing may be salvaged.
BBreak for parts. The body shell must be crushed, but parts may be reused.Never as a vehicle. Parts only.
S (was Cat C)Structural damage that was repairable. Chassis, crumple zones, suspension mounts.Yes, once repaired.
N (was Cat D)Non-structural damage. Cosmetics, electrics, trim, water damage, sometimes theft recovery.Yes, once repaired.

The S and N categories replaced C and D in October 2017. Older records may still show C and D, which map roughly to S and N respectively.

If a car is advertised as Category A or B and is being driven, something is seriously wrong. Either the seller is lying about the category or the vehicle should not exist. There is no legitimate version of that transaction.

Cat S and Cat N in practice

These are the two you will actually encounter, and they are not equivalent.

Category N is often minor. A stolen and recovered car with a smashed window and a ripped-out ignition can be Cat N. So can a car with flood damage to the interior, which is a very different proposition. The category alone does not distinguish between them, which is exactly why you need to ask what the damage was.

Category S means the structure was damaged. Done properly, on a jig, by a competent body shop, a Cat S repair can be sound. Done badly, the car will never track straight, will eat tyres, and will not protect you properly in another impact. You cannot tell which you are looking at from photographs.

What to ask for, in writing:

  • What was the damage, and where?
  • Who repaired it, and is there an invoice?
  • Was it repaired on a jig, and is there an alignment printout?
  • Has it had an independent inspection since?

A seller who has genuinely had a proper repair done keeps the paperwork, because it is the only thing that protects the value. A seller with no paperwork is asking you to take the risk they were not willing to document.

What it does to the money

  • Value. Expect roughly 20% to 40% below a clean equivalent, more for Cat S than Cat N, and more on desirable cars where buyers have choices.
  • Resale. The category stays with the vehicle for life. You will face the same discount when you sell, and a smaller pool of buyers.
  • Insurance. Some insurers decline recorded write-offs outright. Others load the premium. Get a quote before you buy, not after.
  • Finance. Many lenders will not finance a Cat S or N vehicle, which shrinks the buyer pool again.

None of that makes it a bad buy. A properly repaired Cat N car at 30% off, bought to keep for years, can be excellent value. It is a bad buy if you paid a clean-history price, or if you need to sell it in eighteen months.

How you find out, honestly

This is where we have to be straight with you about the limits of a free check.

An MOT history will not tell you a vehicle was written off. Our checker is free and it shows every test, mileage reading and advisory since 2005, which is genuinely useful and catches a lot. But write-off records come from the insurance industry register, finance records come from lenders, and stolen markers come from the police. None of that is public data and no free service has it.

What the MOT history can do is give you a reason to look harder:

  • A gap of a year or more between tests is consistent with a vehicle sitting in a compound and then being repaired. It has innocent explanations too, but it is worth a direct question.
  • A sudden change in advisory pattern, for example steering or suspension alignment issues appearing after a quiet history.
  • A test at a garage a long way from the previous ones, which can indicate the vehicle moved through the salvage trade.

Start with the free MOT history check and read the clocking guide while you are there, because the same trail answers both questions. If the car is expensive, or the history has a gap you do not like, pay for a full vehicle history check before you hand over money. On a £8,000 car it is the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.

The verdict

Category A and B are not road vehicles and never will be. Category S and N are legitimate buys at the right price with the right paperwork, and expensive mistakes without it. Ask what the damage was, ask who repaired it, get an insurance quote before you commit, and never pay clean-history money for a recorded write-off.

title: Lorry and Trailer Annual Tests: The 3,500kg Line That Decides Whether Your Van Gets an MOT or an HGV Test
desc: When a van stops getting an ordinary MOT and starts getting a DVSA annual test, the 2026 fees for lorries and trailers, the electric van exception that runs to 4,250kg, and the 14 day retest window that is worth real money.
body:
The short version
  • At 3,500kg design gross weight a van stops getting an ordinary MOT and starts getting a DVSA annual test. The cost roughly triples and the first test comes two years earlier.
  • The exception almost nobody quotes: a zero emission goods vehicle stays on the ordinary MOT up to 4,250kg. Same size van, electric instead of diesel, and you stay in the cheap lane.
  • Lorries, buses, coaches and trailers are tested every year from year one. Cars, vans and motorcycles get their first MOT at three years.
  • Retest inside 14 days and you pay a fraction of the fee. Day 15 and you pay the whole thing again.
  • Trailers are tested in their own right, with their own record, whatever is towing them.

The 3,500kg line, and what happens when you cross it

Most people running a van never think about this until they upsize. The moment the design gross weight goes past 3,500kg, the vehicle leaves the MOT system that cars, vans and motorcycles sit in and joins the annual test system that lorries, buses and trailers sit in. Different fee, different timetable, different place, different paperwork.

Here is the whole picture in one table. All figures are the GOV.UK maximum MOT fees and the DVSA annual test fees at authorised testing facilities, the latter last updated on 15 July 2026.

VehicleTestFirst test dueFee
Motorcycle, any engine sizeMOT class 1 or 23 years£29.65
Car, up to 8 seatsMOT class 43 years£54.85
Goods vehicle up to 3,000kgMOT class 43 years£54.85
Goods vehicle over 3,000kg up to 3,500kg, petrol, diesel or hybridMOT class 73 years£58.60
Zero emission goods vehicle 3,501kg to 4,250kgMOT class 73 years£58.60
HGV, 2 axlesDVSA annual test12 months£91
HGV, 3 axlesDVSA annual test12 months£113
HGV, 4 or more axlesDVSA annual test12 months£137

Read the two bold rows against the row above them. A 3,500kg diesel Luton pays £58.60 once every year, and nothing at all for its first three years. A 3,600kg diesel version of the same vehicle is an HGV: £91 a year, starting twelve months after it was first registered with DVLA. An electric 4,250kg version pays £58.60 and waits three years.

That zero emission threshold exists because a battery pack is heavy, and without it every electric van would have been pushed into the HGV regime by its own batteries. If you are running a small fleet and weighing up diesel against electric, this belongs in the sums alongside the clean air zone charges, because it moves in the same direction.

The real cost, including the fee nobody quotes

The £91 is not what you pay. Annual tests are carried out by DVSA assessors, but usually at a private site called an authorised testing facility, and the ATF is allowed to charge you separately for the use of its pit. GOV.UK caps that service charge:

Vehicle typeMaximum ATF service charge
HGV£70
Trailer£50

So a two axle lorry can cost £161 at the gate rather than £91, and a two axle trailer £104 rather than £54. That is the number to budget against. The ATF may charge two service charges if a dangerous goods test and an MOT happen in the same visit.

Trailer test fees at an ATF, for comparison:

TrailerAnnual testRetest within 14 daysAverage test length
1 axle£41£1820 minutes
2 axles£54£2525 minutes
3 axles£64£3330 minutes
4 axles£64£3335 minutes
5 axles£64£3340 minutes

Notice that the fee stops rising after three axles but the test gets longer. If you are booking a five axle trailer, book the slot generously.

The 14 day rule is worth real money

This is the single most actionable thing in the fee tables, and it is not signposted anywhere obvious.

If your vehicle fails and you bring it back within 14 days, you pay a reduced retest fee. Bring it back on day 15 or later and you pay the full annual test fee all over again.

VehicleFull testRetest within 14 daysRetest after 14 daysYou lose
HGV, 2 axles£91£35£91£56
HGV, 3 axles£113£49£113£64
HGV, 4 or more axles£137£65£137£72
Trailer, 2 axles£54£25£54£29

There is also a part-paid retest, £13 for an HGV and £7 for a trailer, which covers the narrow case where only a small part of the test has to be repeated.

Miss the window on a four axle unit and a trailer in the same week and you have thrown away roughly £100 for no reason other than scheduling. If a vehicle fails on a Friday, the repair booking matters more than the repair itself.

Prohibitions, which are not the same as a failure

A failed annual test is a planned, budgeted event. A prohibition is not.

DVSA and the police can carry out roadside spot checks, and where they find something serious enough they can issue a prohibition, which stops the vehicle being driven until the fault is put right. Clearing it needs a separate inspection, and that carries its own fee depending on how serious the fault was.

The practical point for anyone buying a used lorry, van or trailer: a clean annual test record is a snapshot taken once a year at a booked appointment, with the operator knowing the date months in advance. It tells you the vehicle can be got through a test. It does not tell you what state it is in on an ordinary Tuesday.

Where the records live, and what you can see for free

Good news, and it surprises people: the free DVSA MOT history service covers heavy vehicles too, not just cars and motorcycles. GOV.UK lists "check the MOT history of a vehicle" as one of the services under its own HGV, bus and trailer testing section, with records going back to 2005.

That means you can put a lorry or trailer registration into our free MOT history checker and get the same thing you would get for a car: the test dates, the results, the reasons for failure and the advisories. For a trailer this matters more than people expect, because a trailer is tested in its own right and carries its own record regardless of what has been towing it. Buy a tidy looking trailer with a bad history and you have bought the history.

What to read for, in order:

  • Gaps in the annual test dates. A heavy vehicle should be tested every year without exception. A missing year means it was off the road, and on a working vehicle that is unusual enough to ask about.
  • Repeat failures on the same item. Brakes and suspension appearing year after year say the vehicle is being patched to a pass rather than maintained.
  • Corrosion advisories. On a trailer chassis these are the expensive ones.
  • Mileage that does not fit the work. The same reading logic applies as on any vehicle. Our guide on reading a used van MOT history covers the method, and it scales up.

If you are choosing between two vehicles you can compare their records side by side before you travel to see either of them. And if you want the general background on what causes failures across all classes, what actually fails an MOT in the UK is the place to start.

The verdict

If you are running vehicles under 3,500kg, none of this applies to you and you do not need to do anything. Your van gets an ordinary MOT at three years and £58.60 a year after that.

If you are about to cross that line, do three sums before you sign. Add the ATF service charge to the headline test fee, because that is the real annual cost. Put every test date in the diary with a repair slot already blocked out inside 14 days, because that window is worth £56 to £72 per failure. And if the vehicle you actually need is a large van rather than a lorry, check whether the electric version keeps you under the 4,250kg zero emission threshold, because staying in class 7 is worth more than the test fee difference alone once clean air zones are counted.

The test record itself is free to read for every one of these vehicles. Read it before you buy, not after.

title: Motorcycle MOT in 2026: What the DVSA Data Says Really Fails a Bike, and What the Test Never Checks
desc: Lamps cause 41% of motorcycle MOT defects but tyres cause 34% of the dangerous ones. The official DVSA figures, the tread rule that is different on a bike, the four things an MOT never inspects, and how to read a used bike's history.
body:
The short version
  • Motorcycles pass first time more often than cars. The DVSA initial failure rate for classes 1 and 2 was 14.00% across 2024 to 2025, against roughly one in four for cars.
  • Lamps and reflectors cause 40.80% of all motorcycle MOT defects. Almost all of it is a bulb, an aim or a missing reflector.
  • Tyres cause only 8.83% of defects but 34.12% of the dangerous ones. That is the single most useful number on this page. The thing that usually fails you is trivial. The thing that usually makes the bike unrideable is the tyres.
  • The legal tread rule for a bike is not the car rule. It is 1mm across three quarters of the breadth, not 1.6mm.
  • An MOT never looks at the engine, clutch or gearbox. A clean pass is not a clean bike.

What the DVSA figures actually say

Most motorcycle MOT advice is somebody's opinion about what garages look for. This is not. The table below is the official DVSA breakdown of initial test failures for MOT classes 1 and 2, full financial year 2024 to 2025, published as part of the MOT testing data series.

Read the last two columns against each other, because that is where the story is.

Defect categoryShare of all defectsShare of dangerous defects
Lamps and reflectors40.80%18.94%
Brakes18.62%25.72%
Structure and attachments11.30%10.10%
Suspension9.79%3.34%
Tyres8.83%34.12%
Steering5.87%6.70%
Identification of the vehicle3.85%not recorded as dangerous
Wheels0.70%1.09%
Horn0.25%not recorded as dangerous

Source: DVSA, MOT class 1 and 2 vehicles, initial failures by defect category, financial year 2024 to 2025 total. Figures checked August 2026.

Lamps and reflectors are the loudest number and the least important one. A blown bulb, a headlamp aimed wrongly after a fork rebuild, a reflector that fell off. Annoying, cheap, and it says almost nothing about the state of the motorcycle.

Tyres are the opposite. They cause about one defect in eleven, but more than a third of everything a tester grades as dangerous. A dangerous defect means you are not supposed to ride the bike away, and 4.39% of all motorcycle tests in that year produced one. So roughly one rider in twenty-three turned up on a bike the tester judged unfit to leave on.

If you take one thing from the data, it is this: spend your pre-test attention on the tyres and the brakes, and fix the bulbs in five minutes the night before. Our guide to what dangerous, major and minor actually mean explains why that grading matters more than the pass or fail line.

The tread rule for a bike is not the car rule

This catches out people who have driven cars for twenty years and then bought a motorcycle. The 1.6mm figure everyone knows is a car figure. It does not apply to your bike.

VehicleLegal minimum tread
Car, van, light trailer1.6mm across the central three quarters, all the way round
Motorcycle over 50cc1mm across three quarters of the breadth, with visible tread on the remaining quarter
Motorcycle or moped up to 50ccAll the grooves of the original tread pattern must be clearly visible

Two practical points. First, the bike limit is lower, which sounds generous until you remember that a motorcycle has two contact patches the size of a credit card and no fourth wheel to save it. Legal and sensible are a long way apart here, and most riders change well before 1mm.

Second, on a small moped there is no depth figure at all. The test is simply whether the original pattern is still visible. A worn scooter tyre can be legal on depth on a 125 and illegal on a 49cc machine with the same tread left.

Tyre age is not part of the MOT, and there is no legal age limit for a private motorcycle tyre. A tyre with plenty of tread and hard, crazed sidewalls will pass. Worth knowing before you buy a low mileage bike that has stood for six years.

What a motorcycle MOT never checks

An MOT is a roadworthiness test at a moment in time. It is not an inspection, it is not a service, and it is not a mechanical opinion. The things it does not cover are exactly the things that cost the most to put right.

  • The engine. Beyond a look for leaks (there is no emissions test in a motorcycle MOT), internal engine condition is not assessed at all. A bike burning oil and rattling on the cam chain can pass.
  • The clutch. Wear, plate thickness and how much life is left in it are not part of the test.
  • The gearbox. The tester needs to be able to move the machine, but general gearbox condition is not inspected.
  • Everything that is a service item. Oil condition, coolant, brake fluid condition, filters, battery health, valve clearances, head bearings that are merely stiff rather than loose.

Chain and sprockets sit in between and confuse people. The tester does look at the final drive: excessive slack, a badly worn chain, worn sprockets or a missing guard can all fail a bike. What the tester is not doing is measuring how much life is left. A chain right at the edge of acceptable will pass and then need replacing a month later.

So a fresh MOT is not a guarantee about anything except the day it was issued. Anyone selling a bike on the strength of "twelve months MOT" is telling you about the certificate, not the motorcycle.

The failure rate is seasonal, and that tells you something

Split the same DVSA data by quarter and a clear pattern appears.

QuarterInitial failure rate
April to June 202413.47%
July to September 202414.04%
October to December 202415.51%
January to March 202513.92%
April to June 202512.85%

Source: DVSA MOT class 1 and 2 initial failure rates by quarter.

The autumn quarter is consistently the worst, and brakes are the category that moves most: 19.76% of defects in October to December against 17.73% in April to June. That is corrosion. A bike that has been ridden through a wet British autumn, or one that sat all summer with the discs going orange, arrives at the test with seized calipers and pitted discs.

The practical version: if your MOT falls in October or November, do not book it the week it expires. Book early enough that a brake failure does not leave you off the road, and take the bike for a proper ride first so the brakes clean themselves up rather than presenting the tester with a surface rusted disc.

Reading a used bike's MOT history before you buy

The full DVSA record is free, goes back to 2005, and the seller cannot edit it. Put the registration into the free MOT history checker and read it in this order.

  1. The mileage trail. Bikes are seasonal, so an uneven pattern is normal in a way it would not be on a car. What is not normal is a reading lower than the one before it. That is either a clerical error or an odometer that has been wound back, and the method for telling the difference is in our guide to spotting a clocked vehicle.
  2. Very low annual mileage over several years. On a motorcycle this is often sold as a virtue. It is not. Standing is hard on tyres, brake fluid, fork seals, batteries and carburettors, and the tyre age problem above applies directly.
  3. Gaps between tests. A missing year usually means the bike was declared off the road. Sometimes that is a rider who took a winter off. Sometimes it is a bike that failed and sat.
  4. Dangerous defects in the history. These are worth more attention than failures. A dangerous grading means the tester judged the machine unfit to ride away, and on a bike that is usually tyres or brakes.
  5. The same advisory repeating. Corrosion noted on the frame, exhaust or brake pipes two tests running is a bill being scheduled for you.

If you are deciding between two bikes you can compare their records side by side before you travel to see either.

Be clear about what this does not cover. A free MOT history will not tell you whether a motorcycle has outstanding finance, has been written off, or is recorded as stolen. That data comes from lenders, the insurance industry register and the police, and no free service has it. On a cheap bike the MOT trail plus a careful look covers most of the risk. On anything expensive, pay for a full vehicle history check as well.

Fees, first test and the exemptions

VehicleMOT classFirst testMaximum fee
Motorcycle up to 200cc13 years£29.65
Motorcycle over 200cc23 years£29.65
Motorcycle with sidecar, up to 200cc13 years£37.80
Motorcycle with sidecar, over 200cc23 years£37.80
Three wheeled vehicle up to 450kg unladen33 years£37.80

Source: GOV.UK maximum MOT test fees. Checked August 2026.

Those are maximums, not prices. Most garages charge well under them, and you should not pay the cap without ringing round first. The full picture on fees and free retests is in what an MOT actually costs.

Two exemptions worth knowing.

A motorcycle manufactured or first registered more than 40 years ago, and not substantially changed in the last 30 years, is exempt from annual testing as a vehicle of historical interest. You declare it on form V112. The bike still has to be roadworthy, and you can still test it voluntarily, which some owners do because it helps when selling.

Northern Ireland works to a different clock. In Great Britain a new motorcycle needs its first MOT at three years. In Northern Ireland, where testing is done by the DVA at its own centres rather than by private garages, cars and motorcycles are tested from four years old. If you are buying a three year old bike with a Northern Ireland history and no MOT on the record, that is why, and it is not a warning sign.

The verdict

If your bike is under three years old you do not need to do anything yet. If it is not, the honest pre-test list is short: check the tyres properly, ride it far enough to clean the brakes up, and walk round it with the lights on. Those three cover the categories behind most of the defects and nearly all of the dangerous ones.

And when you are buying, remember what a certificate is. Twelve months MOT means the bike met a minimum standard on one morning. The history, which is free and which the seller cannot touch, tells you what it has actually been like to own.

title: Classic Car MOT Exemption in 2026: The 40 Year Rule, Substantial Changes and the V112
desc: Cars, vans and motorcycles over 40 years old can stop having an MOT, but it is a declaration you make, not a status you are granted. The 40 year rule, what counts as a substantial change after the May 2026 guidance update, why the road tax date is different, and what an exempt vehicle does to its own MOT history.
body:
The short version
  • A car, van or motorcycle built or first registered more than 40 years ago does not need an MOT, as long as it has not been substantially changed in the last 30 years.
  • It is not automatic. You declare it, on a V112 form, when you tax the vehicle. Nobody at DVSA decides this for you.
  • The guidance on what counts as a substantial change was updated on 19 May 2026 to state the 30 year window plainly. If you last read it before then, read it again.
  • The MOT exemption date and the road tax exemption date are not the same date. Plenty of vehicles are exempt from one and not the other.
  • Exemption removes the test. It does not remove the duty to keep the vehicle roadworthy, and the fine for driving a dangerous vehicle is still up to £2,500 and 3 penalty points.
  • The honest verdict at the end of this page is that most owners should take the exemption and book the test anyway.

1. The 40 year rule, stated properly

Under the current GOV.UK guidance, a vehicle does not need an MOT if it was built or first registered more than 40 years ago, and no substantial changes have been made to it in the last 30 years. Vehicles that qualify are formally called vehicles of historical interest, or VHIs.

Two things about that sentence catch people out.

First, it is a rolling date, not a fixed one. There is no cut-off year. A car first registered in September 1986 becomes eligible in September 2026. Next year a 1987 car joins it. The old rule that tied exemption to vehicles first registered before 1960 no longer stands on its own, and the guidance says directly that the 40 year rule now includes vehicles previously exempted on that basis.

Second, the qualifying date is built or first registered. For most road cars those dates sit within months of each other. For a vehicle that lingered in a showroom, or was imported years after it was made, they can be a long way apart, so check the V5C before assuming anything.

2. Nobody grants you this. You declare it

This is the most common misunderstanding here, and it costs people money.

There is no letter, no approval, and no inspection. GOV.UK is explicit that you do not have to apply to stop getting an MOT. What you do have to do is declare the exemption when you tax the vehicle, using form V112 for cars, vans and motorcycles, or V112G for large goods vehicles. You still have to tax the vehicle every year even when the tax itself is free.

The burden of proof sits entirely with you. The guidance is blunt: if you cannot confirm that a vehicle has not been substantially changed, you must not claim MOT exemption. That matters most when you have bought a car you did not restore yourself and cannot vouch for what happened to it in 1998.

There is also a separate legal duty to tell DVLA about any change that alters what is printed on the V5C, an engine swap being the obvious one. Notifying that change and then claiming exemption on the same vehicle is a contradiction that is easy to spot.

3. What counts as a substantial change

A change is substantial if the technical characteristics of the main components have changed in the previous 30 years, unless it falls into the acceptable alterations list. For everything other than motorcycles, the main components are the chassis or frame, the monocoque bodyshell, the axles and running gear, and the engine.

ComponentSubstantial changeNot a substantial change
Chassis or frameA different design of chassisA replacement of the same pattern as the original
Monocoque bodyshellA shell of a different patternSame pattern as the original, including sub-frames
Axles and running gearAltering the type or method of suspension or steeringChanges made to improve efficiency, safety or environmental performance
EngineA non-original engine, and a different cylinder count is usually the tellA different capacity of the same basic engine, or an alternative original equipment engine

The acceptable changes list is wider than most owners expect. It is not a substantial change if parts were swapped simply to keep the vehicle going because original type parts are no longer reasonably available, nor if the modification is the kind demonstrably done while that model was in production or within ten years of production ending. Changes made while the vehicle was in commercial use also do not count against it, provided you can prove that is when they happened.

Some vehicles are pushed out of the exemption regardless of age: a registration with a Q prefix, a kit car assembled from different makes and models, a kit conversion, and a reconstructed classic as DVLA defines it. Even then there is a route back in. If such a vehicle is taxed in the historic class and has not been modified in the previous 30 years, it is exempt.

4. The tax date and the MOT date are different, and that surprises people

These two exemptions are constantly confused because they share the number 40. They do not share a rule.

MOT exemptionVehicle tax exemption
TriggerBuilt or first registered more than 40 years agoBuilt before 1 January 1986, claimable from 1 April 2026
Shape of the ruleRolls forward continuously with your vehicle's own dateSteps forward once a year, on 1 April
Do you apply?No application. You declare it when taxingYes. You must apply to move into the historic tax class
Fallback if the build date is unknownFirst registration date is usedRegistered before 8 January 1986

The practical result is a gap. A vehicle first registered in June 1986 passes its 40th birthday in June 2026 and is MOT exempt from that day. It is not yet in the free tax bracket, which currently needs a build date before 1 January 1986, so it waits until April 2027. For the best part of a year the owner pays road tax on a car the state no longer requires to be tested. That is not a flaw in the rules, just two different rules wearing similar clothes.

5. Vans, lorries and buses follow different lines

An ordinary van is treated like a car. Over 40 years old and unmodified, the same exemption applies. Above 3.5 tonnes the rules diverge, and that is the same weight threshold that decides whether a vehicle gets an MOT or a DVSA annual test at all, covered in our guide to lorry and trailer annual tests.

  • Large goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes are exempt from testing if they were first used before 1960 and are currently used unladen. Load one, or tow a laden trailer, and the test requirement comes back.
  • Buses and public service vehicles used commercially are exempt only if pre-1960, and only if not substantially changed.
  • Buses that are not public service vehicles fall back to the ordinary 40 year VHI test.
  • Steam powered vehicles are exempt from testing altogether.

Note the asymmetry: a commercial operator running a 1959 lorry laden gets no exemption, while a private owner taking the identical lorry empty to a show does.

6. What this does to a vehicle's record, and why buyers should care

Here is the part that matters if you are buying rather than owning, and it is rarely mentioned.

An exempt vehicle stops generating MOT history. The annual test is the only routine event that writes a dated, independent mileage reading into a public record. Take the test away and that record simply stops. Run a 1984 car through our free MOT history checker and you may well see a healthy trail of tests ending abruptly in 2024, then nothing at all.

That silence is not a red flag by itself. It usually just means the owner took the exemption. But it changes what you can verify, so change how you look:

  • Read the record up to the point it stops. Everything before the exemption date is still there. The pattern of advisories across the last four or five tests tells you how the car was being kept.
  • Compare the final recorded mileage against the odometer today. This is the one hard check you still have. A car that recorded 61,000 miles at its last test in 2023 and shows 62,400 now is plausible. One showing 58,000 is not, and the ordinary rules for spotting a clocked car apply with more force, not less, because nothing has been independently recording the figure since.
  • Ask whether voluntary tests continued. Some owners keep testing past the 40 year mark, and it shows in the record. That is a good sign about the person as much as the vehicle.
  • Ask what changed and when. A seller who claims exemption but describes a suspension conversion done in 2010 has made two statements that cannot both be true.

7. The verdict: take the exemption, book the test anyway

We usually end these guides by saying you need do nothing. Not this time, and the reason is arithmetic.

The maximum a garage may charge for a car MOT is £54.85, a legal ceiling unchanged since 2010, and many test centres charge well under it. Our guide on what an MOT actually costs covers how to pay less than the cap. Set that against brake pipes, flexible hoses and structural steel that have had four decades to corrode, inspected by somebody with no financial interest in flattering the car. It is the cheapest independent second opinion available on a British road.

Claim the exemption, because it removes a legal deadline and the risk of being caught out by one. That is not a reason to stop having the vehicle looked at.

Two things to be clear about, because guessing would be worse than saying nothing. Your insurer may take its own view: some classic policies ask about a current MOT or a valuation inspection, and there is no general rule covering every policy, so read yours rather than trusting a website. And roadworthiness remains your legal responsibility either way. Using a vehicle in a dangerous condition carries a fine of up to £2,500 and 3 penalty points, and the exemption is no defence.

Frequently asked

Do I still have to tax an exempt vehicle? Yes. You must tax it every year even when the amount due is nothing. Failing to tax it is a separate offence from failing to test it.

Where do I get a V112? From GOV.UK, under "declaration of exemption from MOT". V112G is the version for large goods vehicles.

My car is 41 years old but I restored it with a modern engine. Am I exempt? Almost certainly not, if the swap was within the last 30 years and the engine is not an alternative original equipment unit. A different number of cylinders is the usual giveaway.

Can I have a voluntary MOT on an exempt vehicle? Yes, and the result appears in the public MOT history in the normal way. That is exactly why it is worth doing on a vehicle you may sell later.

Does this apply in Northern Ireland? No. This guidance covers England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland runs its own testing scheme through DVA, with different rules.

Who can rule on whether my particular car is substantially changed? The Federation of British Historic Vehicle Clubs publishes a list of historic vehicle specialists, and the Historic and Classic Vehicles Alliance represents trade specialists. Both are named in the DfT guidance. We are not qualified to rule on an individual vehicle, and neither is any other check website.

title: Car, Van and Trailer Towing Rules 2026: What Needs a Test
desc: A trailer under 3,500kg has no MOT and no history. What cars, vans and lorries that tow really need in 2026, and what the MOT towbar check covers.
body:
The short version
  • A trailer or caravan up to 3,500kg gross weight has no MOT and no annual test in Great Britain. There is nothing to renew and no history to look up.
  • Above 3,500kg a trailer must be plated and tested by DVSA every year, in the same system that tests lorries.
  • If you hold a car licence issued on or after 1 January 1997, you have been able to tow up to a 3,500kg trailer without a separate car and trailer test since December 2021. That test no longer exists in Great Britain.
  • The towbar is inspected at the towing vehicle's own MOT, whether that vehicle is a car, a van or a motorcycle, and a 13 pin electrical socket is functionally tested.
  • Because the trailer keeps no record of its own, the only checkable history in a towing outfit belongs to the vehicle doing the pulling.

Towing is the part of UK vehicle law that changed recently, quietly, and in a direction most people still get wrong. Plenty of advice online was written before December 2021 and is now simply false. At the same time, the thing buyers most want to check, a used trailer or caravan, turns out to be the one item on the road carrying no test record at all. This guide sets out what is actually required in 2026 for cars, vans, motorcycles and lorries that tow, what the MOT does and does not look at, and where the checkable evidence really sits.

The licence rule changed in 2021, and most of the internet has not caught up

The old position: if your car licence was issued on or after 1 January 1997, category B alone let you tow a trailer of up to 750kg maximum authorised mass, or a heavier one only if the whole combination stayed within 3,500kg. Anything beyond that needed a separate category B+E test.

That changed in December 2021. The car and trailer test was withdrawn in Great Britain and category B holders were given the towing entitlement automatically. A category B licence now allows a trailer of up to 3,500kg maximum authorised mass, subject to the towing vehicle's own limits. You do not book a test, apply, or pay anything. DVSA no longer runs the test, so there is nothing to book even if you wanted it on paper.

Three things people get wrong about this:

  • It did not raise anybody's towing capacity. The licence stopped being the constraint, the vehicle did not change. Your car or van still has a manufacturer's maximum towing weight and a gross train weight, and exceeding either is an offence whatever your licence permits.
  • Licences issued before 1 January 1997 were never affected. Those already carry the older grandfathered entitlement, typically up to 8,250kg for the combination.
  • It applies to Great Britain, not the whole UK. Northern Ireland kept its car and trailer test. If you learned to drive in Northern Ireland and hold an NI licence, check your entitlement rather than assuming the GB rule covers you.

Losing the test also removed the only formal competence check in the system. Voluntary accredited training is a sensible few hundred pounds if you have never reversed an outfit, but it is optional and it puts nothing on your licence.

Which trailers need a test, and which need nothing at all

This is the table that settles most arguments. Note how much of it says nothing is required.

What you are towing or drivingPeriodic test requiredWho tests it
Trailer or caravan up to 3,500kg gross weightNone. No MOT, no annual test, everNobody
Trailer over 3,500kg gross weightDVSA annual test, and the trailer must be platedDVSA or an authorised testing facility
Car or van up to 3,000kg design gross weight, towbar fittedClass 4 MOT, towbar included in the inspectionMOT station
Van 3,000kg to 3,500kg design gross weightClass 7 MOT, towbar includedMOT station
Goods vehicle over 3,500kgDVSA annual testDVSA or an authorised testing facility
Motorcycle pulling a trailerClass 1 or class 2 MOT on the bikeMOT station

A trailer over 3,500kg must have its first annual test before the end of the month one year after it was first sold or supplied, then once a year after that, and it is issued with a ministry plate showing its weights. The fees, the retest window and the 3,500kg boundary itself are covered in our guide to lorry and trailer annual tests and the 3,500kg line.

Everything below that line, which is the overwhelming majority of caravans, box trailers, plant trailers and boat trailers on British roads, is tested by nobody at any point in its life. The Construction and Use regulations still apply, so brakes, lights, tyres and coupling must be in working order and DVSA can stop you for them. There is simply no annual appointment that proves it.

A trailer has no MOT history, so check the vehicle pulling it

This is the practical consequence for anyone buying used, and it is rarely spelled out. A car with a ten year history gives you a mileage trail, advisories, a failure record and dates you can cross reference. A trailer gives you none of that, because no test was ever recorded against it. There is no database to query and no free checker, ours included, that can produce a trailer's past.

So the checkable evidence sits entirely on the vehicle side. Run the registration through the free MOT history checker and look for the things that matter to a vehicle that has worked:

  • Repeated rear suspension and brake advisories. A car that has spent years pulling a loaded trailer tends to show it at the back first.
  • Mileage that jumps in large annual blocks then flattens. Towing mileage is hard mileage, and a flat recent year on a high total often means the car has been sitting.
  • Corrosion advisories near the rear chassis or the towing point. Once a tester starts writing that down, it does not reverse.
  • Gaps in the record. The same reading rules apply as for any working vehicle, and we set them out in the guide to reading a used van's MOT history.

For the trailer itself you are back to physical inspection. Check the chassis number against the paperwork, read the plate for gross and nose weight, look for weld repairs on the A frame, and read the four digit date code moulded into each tyre. A code of 2718 means week 27 of 2018.

On tyre age, be careful what you read elsewhere. The ban on tyres over ten years old, in force since 1 February 2021, applies to the front steered axles of heavy goods vehicles, buses and coaches, and to all single wheels on minibuses. It sets no legal age limit for a caravan or light trailer tyre. It did require the date code to be legible on heavy vehicles and trailers over 3.5 tonnes. For a caravan, age is a maintenance judgement, not a legal test, and those tyres usually fail from standing rather than from tread wear.

What the MOT actually checks on a vehicle that tows

The towbar is not ignored. Under the MOT inspection manual the tester examines the coupling for security, condition and excessive corrosion, on cars, vans and light commercials alike. Tow ball covers are removed so the ball can be seen, and couplings hidden behind bumper panels are inspected if the panel moves without tools. Fifth wheel couplings are included. Towing eyes, the recovery points, are not tested.

The electrical side splits in two, and this catches people out:

  • A 7 pin socket is checked for safe condition and safe cabling only. Its function is not tested.
  • A 13 pin socket is checked for condition and its electrical connections are functionally tested.

So a car can pass its MOT with a 7 pin socket that does not actually light the trailer. Test it yourself with a board or with the trailer connected before you rely on it.

One more common question: fitting a towbar does not invalidate your MOT and does not require a new one. The towbar becomes part of the inspection at the next test, that is all.

Registering a trailer to take it out of the UK

This is separate from testing, and it is the one piece of paperwork owners genuinely do need to think about. To drive to or through most European countries you must register the trailer with DVLA and display its own number plate.

  • Mandatory for commercial use trailers over 750kg gross weight travelling internationally.
  • Mandatory for non-commercial trailers over 3,500kg gross weight travelling internationally.
  • Voluntary for non-commercial trailers of 3,500kg or less. A touring caravan behind a family car does not have to be registered, though some owners do it anyway.

Published fees are £26 to register a trailer for the first time, £21 for a certificate to a new registered keeper, and £10 to replace a lost or damaged one. DVLA posts the certificate and authorises a plate. A handful of countries sit outside the scheme, so check the current DfT list for your route.

Weights, speed limits and lanes

Three numbers decide whether you are legal, and none is on your licence. The trailer's plate gives its maximum gross weight. The towing vehicle's plate and V5C give the maximum towing mass and the gross train weight, which is the whole outfit loaded. Nose weight, the download on the ball, is limited by both towbar and vehicle, and the lower figure wins.

Speed limits for a car or light vehicle towing any trailer, set by the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984 rather than by the size of what you are pulling:

Road typeTowing limitNormal car limit
Built up area30 mph30 mph
Single carriageway50 mph60 mph
Dual carriageway60 mph70 mph
Motorway60 mph70 mph

On a motorway with three or more lanes you must not use the outside lane while towing, unless signs or a lane closure direct you otherwise. The same restriction applies on a three lane dual carriageway when towing a caravan.

The plain verdict

If you tow a caravan or a trailer under 3,500kg behind a car or a van, the honest answer is that you need to do almost nothing. No test to book, no certificate to renew, no licence course to pass, and no registration unless you are leaving the country. Any service selling a trailer test certificate or a trailer history report in that weight class is selling something that does not exist.

Spend the money you saved on paperwork where it matters: tyres, which age out long before they wear out on a trailer that stands for eight months a year, and brakes, which on an overrun coupling are the most neglected item in the outfit.

And when you are buying, remember where the evidence is. The trailer will tell you nothing about its past. The vehicle in front of it will tell you a great deal, free, in about ten seconds.

title: Buying a Used Motorcycle: Why the MOT Record Has Gaps, and Which Gaps Actually Matter
desc: Most bikes are laid up over winter, so a motorcycle MOT history is full of holes that mean nothing. Which gaps are normal, which one should stop you, why low mileage is not automatically good, and how to read the trail. Free checks for cars, vans, motorcycles and lorries.
body:
The short version
  • A gap in a motorcycle MOT record is normal. Most bikes are laid up over winter, so gaps are the default rather than the warning sign.
  • What matters is the shape of the gap, not the fact of one. A repeating seasonal pause is fine. A single long hole in the middle of an otherwise steady record is the one to ask about.
  • A Statutory Off Road Notification is free and, in Great Britain, does not expire. A bike can sit legally off the road for years and leave no trace at all except missing tests.
  • Low mileage is not automatically good on a bike. Tyres, brake fluid, seals and fuel systems degrade by date, not by use, and the MOT has no tyre age limit for motorcycles.
  • A motorcycle MOT is capped at 29.65 pounds, so the cheapest way to settle an argument with a seller is a fresh test rather than a debate.

Why a bike's MOT record does not look like a car's

This site checks the DVSA MOT history for cars, vans, motorcycles, lorries and trailers, and motorcycles are the class where people most often read the record wrong. They apply car logic to it, panic at the gaps, and walk away from a perfectly good bike. Or they do the opposite, see an unbroken record, and assume that means the bike has been looked after.

The difference is simple. A car is usually somebody's only way of getting to work, so it is taxed, tested and insured continuously for its whole life. A bike is very often a second vehicle used between March and October. Come November it goes in the garage, the owner declares it off the road, and it does not reappear on any official record until spring.

So on a car, a missing year is unusual and worth investigating. On a bike it may just be a wet winter and a busy owner. You still need to look, but you are looking for a different shape.

Put the registration into the free MOT history checker and lay the test dates out in order before you read anything else.

What SORN actually does to the record

A Statutory Off Road Notification, almost always shortened to SORN, is a declaration to DVLA that a vehicle is being kept off the public road. Three things about it explain most motorcycle MOT records.

  • It is free. There is no fee to declare a vehicle off the road, and any complete months of tax left on it are refunded automatically to the address on the V5C. Part months are not refunded.
  • In Great Britain it does not expire. Since October 2013 a SORN runs until the vehicle is taxed again. There is no annual renewal, so a bike can sit for five years with nobody having to do anything.
  • It does not require an MOT. A vehicle off the road does not need a valid test, so the owner has no reason to buy one. That is exactly why the gap appears.

The consequence people miss is what happens on the way back. You cannot tax a vehicle in the UK without a valid MOT, so a bike coming off SORN has to be tested before it can be taxed. The narrow exception in section 192A of the Vehicle Excise and Registration Act 1994 lets an untaxed vehicle be ridden on a public road to or from a pre-booked MOT appointment, and nowhere else. The booking has to exist before you set off, the journey has to be direct, and the bike still has to be insured and roadworthy.

Four things a gap can mean, and how to tell them apart

Lay the test dates in a column. An MOT lasts twelve months, so tests should be roughly a year apart. Where they are not, there are only four realistic explanations, and you can usually narrow it down from the record alone.

What the record showsMost likely explanationHow worried to be
Tests roughly annual but always in spring, with occasional years missing entirelySeasonal use. Laid up over winter, and in some years the owner did not get round to putting it back on the road.Normal. This is what most used bikes look like.
A long gap, then a test that passes first time with few or no advisoriesStored properly and recommissioned before the test. Somebody spent money getting it right.Usually a good sign, not a bad one.
A long gap, then a test that fails, then a pass days laterDragged out of a shed and pushed through. The failure list tells you what had to be replaced to get it through, and nothing more.Read the failure items closely. Perished tyres and seized brakes after storage are common and fixable. Structural corrosion is not.
A gap in the middle of an otherwise unbroken, year-round recordSomething interrupted normal use. An accident, a major mechanical failure, or a theft and recovery.This is the one to ask about. A bike used every winter that suddenly stops for two years has a story the advert will not carry.

The record cannot tell you which of those it was. It can tell you that a specific gap exists, which turns a vague question into a precise one. "Why is there no test between October 2022 and April 2025" gets a far better answer than "has it ever been dropped".

Mileage on a bike, and why the car method half works

The mileage trail is still the most useful thing in the record, but three motorcycle-specific traps catch people out.

Replacement clocks are common and legal. Instrument clusters get damaged in drops, get stolen, or simply fail, and a replacement unit starts from wherever it starts. The record then shows a reading lower than the one before it, which on a car would be the classic clocking signature. On a bike it is often a genuine, declarable repair. It is still your job to ask, and a straight seller will tell you the date the clock was changed and roughly what the old one read.

Imports may be recorded in kilometres. The DVSA record stores the unit alongside the number, but adverts, spreadsheets and some checkers strip it. If a bike appears to have covered an implausible distance in one year, check whether you are comparing a kilometre reading against a mile one before accusing anyone of anything.

What still works exactly as it does on a car is the direction of travel. Readings should only ever go up, gaps in testing should line up with gaps in mileage, and a bike that covered 400 miles a year for six years and then 6,000 in one has changed hands or changed purpose. Our guide on how to spot a clocked vehicle sets out the full method, and the parts about ordering readings and checking for reversals apply to bikes without change.

Low mileage is not the same as good condition

This is the single most expensive misunderstanding in used bike buying, and it is the mirror image of the gap problem.

A 2012 machine showing 4,000 miles sounds like a find. What it usually means is that the bike has spent thirteen years standing still, and standing still is hard on almost everything that is not the engine. Rubber perishes, brake fluid absorbs water from the air, fork seals harden, fuel systems gum up, and a chain sitting in one position rusts unevenly.

The part that catches buyers is the tyres. There is no tyre age limit in the motorcycle MOT. The ten year rule introduced in February 2021 applies to the front steered axles of lorries, buses and coaches, and to single wheels on minibuses. It does not cover motorcycles. So a bike can pass its MOT on tyres manufactured a decade ago, with plenty of tread and a hard, glazed surface that behaves very badly on a cold wet roundabout. The four digit code on the sidewall gives the week and year of manufacture, and it costs nothing to look at it while the bike is on the stand.

What to do with the record before you view

  1. Count the gaps and note the months. Tests clustered in March, April and May are the signature of a seasonally used bike.
  2. Read the first test after each long gap. That test is the closest thing you will get to an independent inspection of what storage did to the machine.
  3. Check whether the current MOT is about to expire. A test can be done up to one calendar month minus a day before expiry without losing the anniversary date, so a seller with a bike due in three weeks has no real excuse.

You can run the same record through our free buyer scorecard, which scores mileage consistency, gaps, dangerous defects and repeated advisories out of 100 and shows you every deduction it made. For what actually fails bikes and what the test never inspects at all, read the motorcycle MOT guide.

What the record will not tell you

Be clear about this, because plenty of sites are not. The MOT history shows tests, dates, mileage readings, failures and advisories. It does not show outstanding finance, an insurance write-off, a theft marker, or whether the bike has been exported. Those come from finance houses, the insurance industry register and the police, and no free service holds them.

Two more motorcycle-specific limits. A machine over 40 years old can be declared exempt from the MOT altogether, at which point it stops generating any record at all, which is covered in our guide to the 40 year exemption rule. And a bike stored on SORN for a decade is completely invisible: no tests, no tax, no trail. Absence of bad news is not good news.

The verdict

Do not reject a used bike for having gaps in its MOT history. Almost all of them do, and a bike that has been properly laid up each winter has usually had an easier life than one ridden through five years of road salt. Reject it for a gap that breaks an otherwise year-round pattern and that the seller will not explain, for a mileage reading that goes backwards with no story attached, and for tyres with a date code older than the last general election.

If the seller and the record disagree, a fresh test settles it for a maximum of 29.65 pounds, a fee capped by DVSA and unchanged since 2010. Our guide on what an MOT actually costs has the full fee table and the free retest rules. Checking the record first is free, takes two minutes, and turns a viewing into an interrogation the seller cannot dodge.
