title: MOT Advisories Explained: Which Ones Matter When Buying a Used Car, and What They Cost to Clear
desc: An MOT advisory is not a fail and has no legal deadline. What the common advisories mean on a car, van or bike, roughly what each costs to put right in 2026, and how to read the pattern before you buy.
body:
The short version
  • An advisory is not a fail. The car passed. The tester is telling you that something is wearing and will probably fail next time if nobody touches it.
  • There is no legal deadline on an advisory. Nobody will fine you for ignoring one. The law only cares whether the car is roadworthy on the day, so an advisory on a tyre that later wears below 1.6mm becomes a police matter, not an MOT one.
  • For a used car buyer, the pattern matters more than any single line. The same advisory repeating for three years tells you the previous owner did the minimum.
  • Roughly, a tyre advisory is £45 to £250 to clear, brake pads are £120 to £300, and structural corrosion can cost more than the car. Figures from 2026 price guides, sources below.
  • Every advisory ever recorded on a car, van, motorcycle or lorry is on the free DVSA record. Put the plate into the MOT history checker and read them before you view.

What an advisory actually is

Since 20 May 2018 the MOT test has sorted every defect into four boxes. Dangerous and major are fails. Minor is a pass with a note that the fault must be fixed soon. Advisory sits underneath all three. It is the tester's judgement that a component is wearing, deteriorating or close to a limit, but is not yet bad enough to be a defect under the DVSA inspection manual.

That is the whole of it. The official wording on the certificate is "monitor and repair if necessary", and that is exactly how much weight it carries. The car passed. Nothing is legally required of you. The advisory exists so that you are not surprised in twelve months.

The reason advisories matter to a buyer is different. Every one is recorded in the DVSA database against the registration, forever, and anyone can read them for free. So a used car's advisories are a history of what the previous owners chose not to fix, written by independent testers who had no reason to be kind. Our guide on dangerous, major, minor and advisory explains the four categories in full. This guide is about what to do with the advisory lines once you have them.

What an advisory costs to clear

These are the advisories that appear most often on ordinary cars, with the rough cost of putting them right. The ranges come from the 2026 repair cost guides published by Bumper and Checkatrade, which pool quotes from UK garages. Your car, your postcode and whether you go to a main dealer or an independent will move the number, so treat them as a scale, not a quote.

Advisory wording you will seeWhat it meansRough cost to clear (2026)
Tyre worn close to legal limitTread is near 1.6mm across the central three quarters. Legal today, not for long.£45 to £250 per tyre depending on size and brand
Brake pads wearing thinFriction material is low. Pads are a consumable.£120 to £300 per axle, parts and labour
Brake discs worn, pitted or scoredDiscs are past their best. Usually replaced with the pads.£130 to £375 per axle
Slight oil leak, not excessiveA weep from a seal or gasket. Only a fail if it drips on the ground.Nil to watch it, £100 to several hundred if a seal is replaced
Slight play in a ball joint, track rod end or wheel bearingNormal wear on steering and suspension.£80 to £250 per item
Corroded but not seriously weakened (sill, subframe, brake pipe)Rust has started on something structural or safety critical.Brake pipes £100 to £300. Structural welding £300 upwards, and it can exceed the value of an older car.
Windscreen chip or damage outside the driver's viewCosmetic unless it spreads into the swept area.Often free on comprehensive insurance for a repair, £150 to £500 for a screen

If a car you are looking at has a fail on its record rather than an advisory, the costs are set out in what actually fails an MOT and what it costs to put right. This guide stays on the advisories.

The advisories that matter when you are buying

Sort the advisories on the record into three groups. It takes about two minutes.

Consumables. Tyres, pads, discs, wiper blades, bulbs. These wear on every car on the road. A single advisory for a tyre or a set of pads tells you nothing about the car except that the previous owner had a test coming and did not want to spend money the week before it. Price it into your offer and move on.

Structure and safety. Corrosion on sills, subframes, suspension mounts, chassis legs or brake pipes. Anything with the word "corroded" next to a part that holds the car together or stops it. This is the group that costs real money and, more to the point, gets worse every winter. A corrosion advisory on a five year old car is unusual and worth asking about. On a fifteen year old car it is expected, but you still want to know whether it has been treated or just noted again each year.

Things that leak or move. Oil leaks, coolant leaks, play in joints and bearings. On their own these are wear. What you are looking for is escalation. "Slight oil leak" in 2023, "oil leak" in 2024, then a fail for "oil leak excessive" in 2025 is a car nobody has looked after. The same three lines, still slight, over three years is a car with a weepy seal that the owner sensibly left alone.

The buyer's rule is simple. One advisory is information. The same advisory three years running is a decision the previous owner made, and you are about to inherit it.

The advisories you can safely ignore

Plenty of what appears in the advisory box is padding. Some garages record a great deal, partly because an advisory is a polite way of quoting for work.

  • "Tyre worn close to legal limit" on a car that has clearly had new tyres since. Check the tyres in front of you, not the record.
  • Non-standard or aftermarket parts noted without a defect. Not a fault.
  • Undertray or engine cover missing or insecure. Cosmetic on most cars.
  • Number plate slightly deteriorated. A £20 fix and no reflection on the car.
  • Any advisory more than two tests old that has not reappeared. It was fixed. The record does not delete cleared advisories, so old ones sit there permanently.

You do not need to do anything about any of these before you buy. You also do not need to pay anyone to interpret them. The same free record that shows you the advisory shows you whether it came back the next year, which is the only interpretation that counts.

Read the pattern, not the line

The most useful thing an MOT record does is line up the advisories year by year. Here is what the common patterns mean.

Pattern in the recordWhat it usually meansWhat to do
Advisory one year, gone the nextFixed. The owner acted on it.Nothing. This is what a cared for car looks like.
Same advisory three years runningIgnored. The owner did the minimum.Budget to clear it and ask what else was skipped.
Advisory, then a fail on the same item, then a passLeft until it broke, then fixed under pressure.Normal for a cheap car. Check the fix was done properly.
No advisories at all, ever, on a car over eight years oldEither a very good car, a very lenient tester, or a record that is shorter than it should be.Check for gaps between test dates. A missing year hides more than an advisory would.
A cluster of new advisories after a change of garageA new tester recording what the old one let go.Read the cluster as the true state of the car.

The last row is worth dwelling on. Testers vary. One garage will pass a car with nothing said, another will write down six advisories on the same car the same week. That is why a single test is weak evidence and a run of five tests is strong evidence. A car with low miles and heavy wear advisories has a story, and our guide on how to spot a clocked car covers reading the mileage line by line.

If you want the pattern read for you, the free buy scorecard takes the registration and scores the advisory history, the mileage consistency and the failure record against the car's age, from the same DVSA data and without charging for it.

What to say to the seller

Advisories give you specific questions instead of vague ones. "Has it had any work done" gets a shrug. "The last two tests both advised corrosion on the rear subframe, has that been treated" gets an answer or a silence, and both are useful.

Three questions that come straight off the record:

  1. For every advisory on the latest test, has it been done, and is there a receipt.
  2. For any advisory that repeats, why was it not done.
  3. For any advisory that turned into a fail, who fixed it and what did they replace.

A dealer who says it will be sorted before collection should put that on the invoice.

If you already own the car

The honest answer is that most advisories do not need anything doing today. Tyres and pads need doing before they reach the limit, and you will save money by booking them yourself in a quiet month rather than having them done as an MOT retest under time pressure. Corrosion is the exception. Rust treated in the summer for a hundred pounds is rust that is not welded in the winter for five hundred.

You do not need a paid report or an inspection for a car you already own. Put the plate into the checker and read the last three tests together.

The verdict

An advisory is a free, independent note that something is wearing. It is not a fail, it carries no penalty, and one on its own tells you almost nothing about a car. What tells you a great deal is whether the same advisory comes back year after year, whether it escalated into a fail, and whether it sits on a consumable or on the structure. That pattern is on the free DVSA record for every car, van, motorcycle and lorry in the country, and reading it takes less time than the drive to view the car. Read it first. If you are choosing between two cars, compare them side by side and let the advisories settle it.

Repair cost ranges are taken from the 2026 UK price guides published by Bumper (brake pads £120 to £300, brake discs £130 to £375, tyres £45 to £250) and Checkatrade, checked September 2026. Defect categories and the 1.6mm tread limit are from the DVSA MOT inspection manual for cars and passenger vehicles on GOV.UK.

title: First MOT for a New Car, Van or Motorcycle: When It Is Due, What It Costs and Why It Is Still Three Years
desc: The first MOT is due three years from first registration in Great Britain, four in Northern Ireland, one year for taxis and lorries. Fees, the one month early rule, the £1,000 fine, what fails at three years, and how to buy a car that has no MOT history yet.
body:
The short version
  • A new car, van or motorcycle in Great Britain needs its first MOT by the third anniversary of the date it was first registered, not the date you bought it. In Northern Ireland it is four years.
  • The maximum fee is £54.85 for a car or a van up to 3,000kg, £58.60 for a van between 3,000kg and 3,500kg, and £29.65 for a motorcycle. No VAT. Those caps have not moved since 2010 and most garages charge less.
  • You can test up to a month minus a day early and keep the same anniversary date. Earlier than that and the renewal date moves.
  • The government looked hard at pushing the first test to four years and decided in January 2024 not to. It stays at three. Tyres and brakes are the reason.
  • A vehicle under three years old has no MOT history at all. Put the plate into the MOT history checker and you will see the first test due date and nothing else. That is correct, not a fault, and this guide covers what to check instead.

When the first MOT is actually due

The rule is short. A car, a van up to 3,500kg or a motorcycle first registered in Great Britain must have a valid MOT from the third anniversary of its registration. That date is on the V5C logbook and on the free DVSA record. If the car was registered on 12 September 2023, it needs an MOT certificate in place by 12 September 2026, and it must pass again every year after that.

Two things trip people up. The clock starts at first registration, not at delivery, purchase or the date on the finance agreement. A car that sat in a dealer compound for two months still counts from the registration date. And a used car bought at two and a half years old comes with the same clock. You inherit the previous owner's anniversary. If the seller cannot tell you when it is due, the checker will.

Northern Ireland is different. A car registered there gets its first test at four years. The Department for Transport confirmed in January 2024 that a GB-registered lease or hire car genuinely based in Northern Ireland can be re-registered there and move to the four year cycle. It is not a loophole for a car kept in Manchester.

Vehicles tested at one year, and lorries

Not everything gets three years. The GOV.UK fee table lists the vehicles tested at one year old: taxis and ambulances, private passenger vehicles with nine or more seats, and playbuses. If you are buying a former taxi or a minibus, expect a record that starts at year one, and treat the absence of one as a question for the seller.

Lorries are a different regime. A goods vehicle over 3,500kg does not get an MOT. It gets a DVSA annual test, and the first one is due one year after registration. The same applies to trailers over 3,500kg and to buses and coaches. On a mixed fleet the 3,500kg line decides which vehicle gets three years of grace and which gets one. The detail is in HGV and trailer annual test versus van MOT.

What the first MOT costs

The Department for Transport sets a legal maximum for each class. A garage can charge less, and many do as a hook for servicing work, but not more. No VAT. Figures from the GOV.UK MOT costs page, checked 4 September 2026, unchanged since 2010.

VehicleClassFirst test dueMaximum fee
Car, up to 8 passenger seats43 years£54.85
Van or goods vehicle up to 3,000kg43 years£54.85
Van 3,001kg to 3,500kg (petrol, diesel, hybrid)73 years£58.60
Electric van 3,501kg to 4,250kg73 years£58.60
Motorcycle, any engine size1 or 23 years£29.65
Motorcycle with sidecar1 or 23 years£37.80
Motor caravan43 years£54.85
Taxi or ambulance41 year£54.85
Minibus, 9 to 12 seats41 year£57.30
Minibus, 13 to 16 seats51 year£59.55

The fee is the cheap part. The expensive part of a first MOT is what it finds, which is covered below. If you want the fee side in more detail, including when a retest is free, read how much an MOT costs.

How early you can book without losing the date

You can have the first MOT done up to a month minus a day before the three year anniversary and the certificate will still run to the anniversary of the original date the following year. GOV.UK gives the example directly: a test due on 15 May can be done from 16 April and the next one will still be due on 15 May.

Test it earlier than that and the expiry moves. Take the same car in on 14 April and pass, and the new certificate expires on 13 April next year. You lose the days rather than gaining them. There is no penalty, it is simply how the certificate is dated, but there is no reason to rush a first MOT six weeks early. The same window applies to vans, motorcycles and every later MOT. It does not apply if the previous test was in Northern Ireland and the next is in Great Britain.

What happens if you miss it

From the day after the third anniversary, driving on a public road without a valid MOT is an offence with a fine of up to £1,000. The only exceptions are driving to a pre-booked MOT appointment or to and from a place of repair, and the vehicle still has to be roadworthy. A bald tyre on the way to the test is a separate offence.

Two knock-on effects cost more than the fine. You cannot tax a vehicle without a valid MOT, so if the tax falls due in the same month everything stalls until the test is passed. And most insurance policies require the vehicle to be legally on the road, so an insurer may reduce or refuse a claim. Check your own policy wording.

DVSA runs a free reminder service by text or email, and our MOT reminder page gives you the same date with a calendar download and no sign up. Use one of them. The first anniversary is the one people forget, because there has never been a certificate to look at.

Why it is still three years and not four

The Department for Transport consulted in early 2023 on moving the first MOT for cars, vans and motorcycles from three years to four. The response, published January 2024, records 4,489 replies of which 84 per cent opposed the change, and the government decided not to proceed. That still stands in September 2026, so anyone telling you the first MOT is now at four years is out of date.

The reason is the useful part. The response says tyre and brake wear are the most common reasons for first-time failures, and it publishes DVSA failure rates for three year old cars from 2021.

Fuel typeFailure rate, all ages (2021)Failure rate at first test, age 3 (2021)
Petrol5.70%3.64%
Diesel6.85%5.14%
Electric6.11%5.53%

Two things stand out. A three year old diesel fails half again as often as a three year old petrol. And a three year old electric car fails more often than either, which the consultation attributes to weight and torque wearing tyres faster. One respondent's analysis of DVSA data showed EVs with higher rates of tyre failure at the first test. If your first MOT is on an electric car, the tyres are the single item most likely to catch you.

What actually fails at a first MOT

A three year old vehicle does not have corrosion or a worn suspension bush. What it has is whatever the driver has not looked at. The consultation response names tyres and brakes as the most common first-test failures, and tyre manufacturers who responded said tyres are by a large margin the leading cause of failure for light vehicles aged three to five. Lamps come next, usually a blown bulb or a misaligned headlamp.

The checklist before a first test is short. Tread depth on all four tyres, legal minimum 1.6mm across the central three quarters. Every bulb including number plate lamps. Wiper blades and washer fluid, which are trivially cheap and fail cars every day. Brake pads if you can see them through the wheel, and any dashboard warning light, because a lit engine management, ABS or airbag lamp is a fail in its own right. For a van, add the load area doors and catches, and expect the tyres to have worn faster. For a motorcycle the tread limit is 1mm, and the chain, sprockets and steering head bearings are checked too. There is a fuller list in what fails an MOT.

If it fails, the retest rules soften the blow. Leave the vehicle at the test centre and get it retested within ten working days and there is no fee. Take it away and bring it back before the end of the next working day and a partial retest is free for a fixed list that covers the common first-test items: tyres and wheels (not motorcycles), lamps, mirrors, wipers and washers, seatbelts, horn and number plates. Within ten working days you may be charged a partial fee. After that it is the full fee again.

Buying a car with no MOT history yet

This is the part every other guide skips. A car under three years old has never been tested, so the free DVSA record is empty. The checker shows the first test due date, the make, model, colour and fuel, and nothing else. That is correct output, not a data gap, and no paid report can conjure a test record that does not exist.

What you lose is the one piece of independent evidence every cheap check relies on: a yearly mileage reading taken by someone with no stake in the sale. Without it a clocked nearly-new car is harder to spot, and ex-lease and ex-rental cars can have done 30,000 miles a year. So the work shifts to other paper.

What you cannot getWhat to use instead
Mileage trail from MOT testsEvery service invoice, in date order, with the mileage on each. A lease car should have a full dealer service history. Photograph the odometer at the viewing.
Advisory patternTyre tread and brake pad condition now. On a three year old car these are the only wear items, so inspect them yourself.
Pass and fail historyThe DVSA recall record, which is free and does exist from day one. An outstanding safety recall on a nearly-new car is more telling than any advisory.
Independent confirmation of the registration dateThe V5C and the checker's first-test-due date. If the seller's "2024 car" has a first MOT due in 2026, it was registered in 2023.

One habit that costs nothing. If the car is within a month of its third anniversary, ask the seller to put it through the MOT before you pay. A private seller has no reason to refuse on a sound car. A fresh pass is the cheapest reassurance available, and a refusal tells you something too.

The plain verdict

The first MOT is due three years from first registration in Great Britain, four in Northern Ireland, and one year for taxis, minibuses and anything over 3,500kg. It costs at most £54.85 for a car or small van, £58.60 for a heavier van and £29.65 for a motorcycle, and it is not moving to four years, because the government looked at that in 2024 and said no. Book it inside the last month before the anniversary, check the tyres, bulbs and wipers the weekend before, and it is a £50 formality. Miss it and it is a £1,000 fine, a tax renewal you cannot complete and an insurance conversation you do not want.

If you are buying rather than owning, accept that the record is empty and stop paying for reports that promise otherwise. Read the service invoices, check the recalls, and use the checker for the one thing it can tell you about a nearly-new car: the day the clock runs out.

Fees, first test ages, the one month rule, the £1,000 fine and retest conditions are from the GOV.UK Getting an MOT guide, checked 4 September 2026. Consultation figures and the 2021 failure rates are from the Department for Transport paper Date of the first MOT test: consultation response, January 2024.

title: Buying an Imported Car, Van or Motorcycle: Why the MOT History Starts Blank, What Registration Costs, and What to Check Instead
desc: An imported car, van or motorcycle has no UK MOT history before its DVLA registration, and its readings may be in kilometres. The 14 day NOVA rule, the £55 registration fee, the £199 IVA test, the 10 year exemption, the write-off trap, and how to read an import's record without being fooled.
body:
The short version
  • The free DVSA record only holds MOT tests done in the UK. A car, van or motorcycle that spent its first years abroad shows nothing before its UK registration, however old it is. That is not a gap to worry about, it is how the data works.
  • An import over three years old must pass a UK MOT before DVLA will register it, so the first line on its record is usually dated before the registration date and was recorded against the chassis number. That looks odd and is normal.
  • Odometer readings on the record can be in kilometres. A reading that appears to fall from 120,000 to 75,000 is usually a unit change, not clocking. Check the unit before you accuse anyone.
  • Importing a car costs more than the ferry: a £55 DVLA registration fee, a £199 approval test for most cars under ten years old, £100 for a left-hand drive EU car, plus VAT and duty that depend on where it came from. Figures from GOV.UK, checked 5 September 2026.
  • A vehicle marked as a statutory write-off, scrapped or non-repairable abroad cannot be registered in the UK at all, and nothing you paid on the way is refunded.

Why an import's MOT history starts blank

Put an imported car's registration into the MOT history checker and you will often see a record that begins years after the car was built. A 2019 car brought in from Japan in 2026 shows a 2026 registration date and, at most, one test. Buyers regularly read that as suspicious. It is not. The DVSA record covers tests carried out in the UK against a UK identity, and nothing that happened to the vehicle in Japan, Germany, Ireland or anywhere else is in it. There is no foreign MOT history to import along with the car.

What the record does give you is the date the vehicle was registered here and, where DVLA has it, the date it was first used, which is normally the foreign registration date taken from the original registration certificate. Those two dates can be years apart, and the distance between them is the first thing to note. Everything before the UK date has to be proven by paperwork, not by a database.

One consequence surprises people. The MOT clock runs from the date the vehicle was first used, not from its UK registration. GOV.UK's registration rules say that a vehicle over three years old, four in Northern Ireland, needs evidence of a current MOT before DVLA will register it. So a five year old import has to pass a UK MOT before it has a UK number plate. The tester records that test against the vehicle identification number, and once DVLA issues the registration the test attaches to it. That is why the first test on an import's record is often dated a few weeks before the registration date. If you see that pattern, it is evidence the import was done properly, not evidence of something hidden.

Driving an unregistered import on the road is a prosecutable offence, with one exception: driving it to a pre-booked MOT or approval test. A seller using an import on foreign plates with no UK registration is a reason to walk away.

Kilometres, miles and the mileage trail

The DVSA record stores each odometer reading with its unit, and the checker shows the unit as recorded. Most UK vehicles read in miles. An import with a kilometre odometer will have readings entered in kilometres, at least until someone fits a mile clock or a tester enters the figure in the wrong unit. That produces a record that looks like this.

TestReading as recordedWhat it means
2024 (abroad)Nothing on the UK recordAsk for the export certificate or foreign inspection paperwork
2025 (first UK test)118,400 kmEquivalent to about 73,600 miles
202676,900 miOdometer replaced with a mile unit, or the tester entered miles. Roughly 3,300 miles on from 2025, which is plausible
202779,100 miConsistent

Read that trail in raw numbers and the mileage "fell" by 41,500 between 2025 and 2026. Read it in the right units and it rose by about 3,300. To convert, multiply kilometres by 0.621, or divide by 1.609. The scorecard penalises a reading that falls between tests because on a UK car that is the single most provable sign of clocking. On an import, check the unit column first, then decide. The guide on spotting a clocked car covers the method for the normal case; this is the one situation where the method needs a second step.

The pre-import mileage is a different problem, because no UK database can verify it. For a Japanese import, ask for the export certificate, which records the odometer at deregistration, and the auction sheet if there is one. For an EU car, ask for the last inspection report from that country. DVLA keeps the original foreign registration certificate and does not return it, so a private seller only has a copy if they took one. A seller who can produce none of these is asking you to take the pre-import mileage on trust. Price accordingly.

What importing a vehicle actually involves, and what it costs

If you are buying a car that has already been imported, you do not have to do any of this, but you do need to know it was done, because a vehicle that skipped a step cannot be legally used. If you are importing one yourself, this is the order GOV.UK sets out. All figures are from GOV.UK pages checked on 5 September 2026.

StepWhat it isCost
Tell HMRCA Notification of Vehicle Arrivals (NOVA) declaration within 14 days of the vehicle arriving. DVLA will not register the vehicle until it is processed. Late notification can be fined.No fee for the declaration itself; a shipping company or customs agent may charge to make it for you
VAT and customs dutyDue on most vehicles brought into Great Britain from outside the UK. The rate depends on the vehicle and where it came from. Relief may apply if you are moving to the UK with your own vehicle or returning an exported one.Varies; GOV.UK tells you to confirm the rate with your customs agent or the HMRC helpline
Vehicle approvalIndividual Vehicle Approval (IVA) for a car from outside the EU, or a GB conversion IVA certificate for a left-hand drive car that already has EU approval. Motorcycles use the Motorcycle Single Vehicle Approval scheme.IVA inspection for a personal import car: £199 in working hours, £294 outside, re-inspection £40. GB conversion IVA: £100
MOTRequired before registration if the vehicle is over three years old (four in Northern Ireland).Maximum £54.85 for a car, see what an MOT costs

DVLA may ask to inspect the vehicle.£55 first registration fee, plus vehicle tax. The £55 is waived for a vehicle coming back to the UK that was registered here before
WaitThe V5C log book can take up to six weeks to arrive, and you need it to get number plates made.Time, not money

The ten year rule matters most for buyers of older imports. GOV.UK's exemptions list says cars and vans up to 3,500kg over ten years old do not need vehicle approval, and lorries over 3,500kg are exempt at 25 years. So a 2014 car arriving in 2026 skips the £199 test and a 2018 car does not. If a seller of an under ten year old import cannot show an approval certificate, either DVLA accepted a letter explaining why it was missing, which GOV.UK allows in specific cases, or something was not done. Ask which.

Left-hand drive cars and the headlamp question

A left-hand drive car's dipped beams kick up to the right, which dazzles oncoming traffic here. Section 4.1.2 of the MOT inspection manual accepts masks or converter kits on right-hand dip headlamps as a temporary fix, so a left-hand drive car can pass its MOT on stick-on beam deflectors and does not need new headlamp units to pass. Whether you want to live with deflectors for years is another matter, and UK-pattern LED headlamps for a modern car can cost many times the IVA fee. Get that quote before you buy.

An EU-registered left-hand drive car with a European Certificate of Conformity uses the £100 GB conversion IVA rather than the full inspection. Vans up to 3,500kg can use it too; lorries over 3,500kg cannot and must go through full IVA.

The damage trap, and Q plates

This is the part that costs people real money. GOV.UK is blunt: a vehicle classed as seriously damaged cannot be registered in the UK, and if you paid VAT, duty or an approval fee before finding that out, none of it is refunded. Seriously damaged means the foreign registration document says something like statutory write-off, scrapped or non-repairable, which is the equivalent of the UK's category A or B. The guide to write-off categories explains how the UK classes work. The check has to happen before the vehicle is shipped, by asking the registration authority in the country of origin, because once it is here there is no route back to a registration.

A vehicle whose age or identity DVLA cannot establish may be given a Q registration number instead, and GOV.UK says any original registration then becomes invalid for good. A Q plate is legal to drive, test and insure, but it marks the vehicle as one of unknown history and it never goes away. On an import it usually means the foreign paperwork could not prove the manufacture date. Ask why.

Cars coming back to the UK

A vehicle that was registered here, exported, and is now returning follows a shorter path: tell HMRC within 14 days, pay any VAT or duty due, pass an MOT if it is over three years old, and register with DVLA. No vehicle approval is needed and the £55 fee is not charged. The useful buyer point is that its old UK MOT history still exists under its old registration. Ask the seller what the number was before export and put that into the checker. If the record stops in, say, 2021 and the car is being sold in 2026 as a re-import, the missing years were spent abroad and the same paperwork questions apply to them as to any other import.

What to check on an import instead of the MOT history

Because the record cannot cover the vehicle's earlier life, the paperwork has to. In rough order of how much each one proves:

  • The V5C, showing the UK registration date and the date of first registration abroad. If the two are the same, DVLA did not have the foreign date, which usually means the original certificate was missing.
  • A copy of the original foreign registration certificate, taken before DVLA kept it. It is the only document that proves the manufacture date and country of origin.
  • The IVA or GB conversion IVA certificate if the vehicle was under ten years old when registered, or a plain explanation of why none exists.
  • NOVA confirmation from HMRC. A registered vehicle must have had one, so its absence is a paperwork failure rather than a legal one, but ask.
  • An export certificate or foreign inspection report showing the odometer reading when the vehicle left its home country, in the unit used there.
  • The outstanding recall flag on the free record, which applies to imports once registered because DVSA carries it in the same data.
  • Every UK test since registration, read with the unit column, using the checker and the scorecard.

Plain verdict

A blank or short MOT history on an import is not a red flag. It is the correct output of a system that only records UK tests, and an import that was registered properly will show a first test dated just before its registration and readings that may be in kilometres. The red flags are elsewhere: a seller who cannot produce a copy of the foreign registration document, a recent import with no approval certificate, a mileage story that only exists verbally, and any hint of write-off wording on the overseas paperwork. Those are the questions to ask, and none of them can be answered by paying for a report that draws on the same UK data you can already see free. Use the MOT history checker for what it can prove, which is everything since the UK number plate went on, and use paper for everything before that.

Import steps, the 14 day NOVA rule, VAT and duty rules, the £55 registration fee, the six week V5C timescale, the ten year and 25 year approval exemptions, the £100 GB conversion IVA fee, the seriously damaged rule and the Q plate rule are from the GOV.UK guides Importing vehicles into the UK, Vehicle approval and Vehicle registration, checked 5 September 2026. IVA fees are from the DVSA publication Vehicle approval test costs: cars (M1), updated 13 December 2022 and still current at the time of checking. The headlamp rule is from section 4.1.2 of the DVSA MOT inspection manual for cars and passenger vehicles.

title: DVSA roadside checks on vans: what officers look for, what it costs, and what the MOT history shows first
desc: What a DVSA or police roadside stop covers for a van, the fixed penalties and prohibitions from GOV.UK, the 2024 to 2025 prosecution figures, and how a cleared prohibition shows up in the MOT history of a car, van or lorry before you buy.
body:
DVSA and the police can pull over any van on any road and inspect it on the spot, in the same way they stop lorries and coaches. Most van drivers, and most people buying a used van, have no idea what that check covers, what it costs when it goes wrong, or that the outcome can end up written into the vehicle's MOT record. This guide sets out what the officer is looking for, the fixed penalties and prohibitions as published by GOV.UK and the Fixed Penalty Order, the 2024 to 2025 prosecution figures, and the two places a roadside check leaves a trace that a free MOT history check can show you before you buy. It applies to vans up to 3,500kg; cars are covered by most of the same defect rules, and lorries have their own regime, which we cover in the HGV annual test guide.

  • DVSA officers and the police can stop vans, lorries, buses and coaches for a spot check, at the roadside or at a check site. Not stopping is itself an offence.
  • The check covers roadworthiness, load weight and how the load is secured, and, where they apply, driver's hours and the operator's licence.
  • Roadside fixed penalties run from £50 to £300 per offence, and some carry three penalty points. Defective brakes are the GOV.UK example: £100 and three points.
  • Overloading is graduated: £100, £200 or £300 depending on how far over the plated weight the van is, with an immediate prohibition on top. Over 30 percent goes to court.
  • In 2024 to 2025, 300 of the 448 van offences DVSA reported for prosecution were overloading, up 55 percent on the year before, with a 98 percent conviction rate.
  • A prohibition cleared by a full inspection produces a new MOT certificate, so an unexplained mid-year MOT pass in the history can be the footprint of a roadside stop.

Who can stop a van, and what happens

The GOV.UK guide Roadside checks for HGV, van, bus or coach drivers, last updated 2 September 2026, is plain about the scope: the police and DVSA officers "can stop vans, lorries, buses and coaches". A DVSA officer wears a yellow visibility jacket with the DVSA logo, drives a vehicle with black and yellow markings and the logo on the bonnet, and always carries a warrant card. If you are carrying a high value load you are allowed to keep the engine running and the doors locked until you are satisfied the person is genuine.

The check itself happens either at the roadside or at a dedicated site the officer directs you to. The officer checks the authorised load weight and the type of load permitted, the mechanical condition of the vehicle, tachograph records where the vehicle needs one, and that the driver holds the right licence. If you do not stop when a uniformed officer asks you to, the incident is recorded, you are interviewed later, and you can face court or referral to the Traffic Commissioner.

One point worth stating because so many van drivers get it wrong: none of this depends on the van having an operator's licence. A sole trader in a 2016 Transit with no O licence can be stopped, weighed, inspected and fined in exactly the same way as a fleet vehicle. The operator's licence only changes what happens afterwards, since licensed operators are reported to the Traffic Commissioner and unlicensed ones are not.

What the officer actually looks at

DVSA publishes the walkaround it expects a van driver to do before every journey, in the guidance Carry out van daily walkaround checks, published 8 October 2013 and still current. A roadside inspection follows the same list, because the officer is checking whether you did it. The sixteen items are, inside the cab: front view and mirrors, washers and wipers, dashboard warning lights (ABS, airbag, ESC, parking brake), steering, horn, brakes and seat belts. Outside: lights and indicators, fluids and leaks, battery, bodywork and doors, tyres and wheels, load security, AdBlue level, exhaust smoke and noise, and any alternative fuel system.

The same guidance names the defects officers find most often on vans: tyres, lights and reflectors, suspension, steering and transmission. It also carries the line that most van drivers have never read: "You can get 3 penalty points on your licence for each tyre that is not safe and legal." On a van with four worn tyres that is twelve points from one stop, which is a ban.

Fines, points and what they cost

The fixed penalty amounts come from the Fixed Penalty Order 2000 as amended by the Fixed Penalty (Amendment) Order 2013, which raised every graduated roadside penalty on 16 August 2013 and has not been changed since. GOV.UK summarises the range as £50 to £300 per offence at the roadside, with court for anything more serious.

Offence at a roadside checkFixed penaltyPointsSource
Defective brakes£1003GOV.UK roadside checks guide, worked example
Each unsafe or illegal tyreUsually £100 at the roadside; up to £2,500 per tyre if it goes to court3 per tyreGOV.UK van walkaround guidance; Road Traffic Act 1988 section 41A
Overloaded by 5 to 10 percent£100NoneFixed Penalty Order 2000, Schedule 2, table 5, as amended 2013
Overloaded by 10 to 15 percent£200NoneSame
Overloaded by 15 to 30 percent£300NoneSame
Overloaded by more than 30 percentCourt, no fixed penaltyCourt decidesDVSA enforcement policy
Other non-endorsable offences£50NoneFixed Penalty Order 2000, item 27

Two mechanics of the scheme matter more than the headline numbers. First, a UK driver has 28 days to pay or to ask for a court hearing. Miss both and the penalty goes up by half and the court recovers it. Second, if you do not have what GOV.UK calls a satisfactory UK address, which excludes hotels, agency and solicitor addresses, you pay a financial penalty deposit on the spot, either the total of the fixed penalties or £500 per offence going to court, capped at £1,500, and the van is immobilised until you do. That catches a surprising number of drivers on temporary contracts.

The overloading figures are the ones a van buyer should keep in mind, because a van's real payload is often far smaller than its size suggests. The plated maximum authorised mass on the sticker in the door shut is the whole vehicle including driver, fuel, racking and load. A 3,500kg van with a 2,200kg kerb weight, 150kg of racking and a 90kg driver has about 1,060kg left for tools and materials. A pallet of plasterboard or a builder's bag of sand uses most of that. Officers weigh the van on portable pads or direct it to a weighbridge; the tolerance before any penalty is 5 percent unless the excess is a tonne or more.

Prohibitions: immediate, delayed and S marked

A fine is the smaller half of the cost. The larger half is the prohibition notice, which stops the van being used until the defect is fixed and the notice is cleared. GOV.UK sets out three flavours.

An immediate prohibition means the van does not move. It is issued for dangerous defects and for every overloading case: the notice says plainly that an overloaded vehicle gets an immediate prohibition and may be immobilised, though the officer can direct it somewhere nearby to shed load. A delayed prohibition lets you drive away and gives the operator up to ten days to fix the problem, with the clock set by severity: up to three days for more than one defect in a safety critical area such as brakes, lights or steering, four to seven days for one critical defect or five or more non-critical ones, and up to ten days for fewer than five non-critical defects. An S marked prohibition is the serious one. It is issued when the defect points to a maintenance failure rather than something that happened on the journey, DVSA follows it with an assessment of the operator's maintenance system, and an immediate S marked notice usually means the van is immobilised and prosecution follows.

A van towing a trailer is treated as two units, so it can collect two prohibitions in one stop. The GOV.UK guide also notes that you would not get an S mark for a defect you could not have known about before setting off, for example something underneath the van that a walkaround would not reveal.

Clearing a prohibition, and why it shows in the MOT history

This is the section that matters if you are buying rather than driving. To lift a prohibition the vehicle has to be inspected again, and the notice states whether a partial or a full inspection is required. GOV.UK says a full inspection "is the same as an MOT", and that when it passes you get a new MOT certificate lasting 12 months, or 13 months if the inspection fell within a month of the old certificate expiring, along with the prohibition removal notice. A partial inspection covers the prohibited items plus brakes and steering, and leaves the existing MOT date untouched.

So a van that was prohibited at the roadside in, say, February, with an MOT that was not due until September, comes out of the full inspection with a fresh MOT pass dated February. On the free MOT history checker that appears as an extra test in the trail, seven months early, usually a pass, sometimes with advisories that match the reason for the stop. Most buyers read an early pass as a careful owner. On a working van it is at least as likely to be the footprint of a roadside prohibition.

What the MOT trail showsInnocent readingRoadside readingWhat to ask
A pass several months before the previous certificate expiredOwner tested early before a long trip or a saleFull inspection to clear a prohibitionWhy was it tested early, and can you show the prohibition removal notice
Early pass with tyre, brake or suspension advisoriesRoutine wearThe defects the officer found, fixed just far enough to passInvoices for the repairs, not just the certificate
Repeated rear spring, rear tyre and brake imbalance advisoriesHeavy useHabitual overloading, the offence that made up two thirds of van prosecutions in 2024 to 2025What was the van used for, and was it ever weighed
A failure followed by a pass the same day at a different stationRetest after repairNot roadside related, but worth checking the mileage did not moveWhere was the repair done

The second trace is not on the MOT record at all. DVSA holds prohibition and encounter history against the vehicle for its Operator Compliance Risk Score, and a van with a recent prohibition is more likely to be stopped again. That history does not transfer to a buyer's name, but it does travel with the registration, which is one more reason to check a working van's MOT trail properly rather than glance at the expiry date.

What DVSA actually prosecuted in 2024 to 2025

DVSA's enforcement data for the 2024 to 2025 financial year, analysed by Tempcover in August 2026, gives the shape of what a roadside stop finds on a van when it goes as far as court. Of 448 light goods vehicle offences reported for prosecution, 300 were overloading, a 55 percent rise on the 193 the year before. Construction and use offences, which is the legal heading for vehicle condition, were second at 95. Plating and testing, which covers expired or missing MOT certificates, was 10. The conviction rate across all 448 was 97 percent, and for overloading 98 percent, so once a case is reported it is almost never lost.

Two cautions on these numbers. They count only cases reported for prosecution, not fixed penalties or prohibitions, which are far more numerous and are not published in the same form. And the "average fine" figures circulating from the same analysis are sums of quarterly averages rather than a fine any one driver paid, so we have not repeated them. The plain reading is enough: overloading is the offence that gets a van to court, and it is the one that a buyer can partly detect from the wear pattern in the MOT record.

Before a long motorway drive: what is worth doing and what is not

The walkaround is free and takes five minutes, and it covers every item an officer will look at first. Tyre pressures and tread on all four plus the spare, all lights including the high level brake light and number plate lamp, washer fluid, AdBlue if the van uses it, and a load that cannot shift. If the van is close to its plated weight, the only reliable answer is a public weighbridge, which GOV.UK lists by area under Find a weighbridge, and which charge a small fee per weighing.

What is not worth paying for: a pre-trip "safety inspection" from a garage that is really a visual check of the same sixteen items. If the van has a current MOT with no dangerous or major defects recorded and the walkaround is clean, a further paid inspection adds nothing an officer would find. Check the MOT and days remaining on the reminders page, and if you are looking at a van to buy, run it through the scorecard, which flags the mileage and advisory patterns described above automatically.

Plain verdict

If you drive a van: do the DVSA walkaround before every journey, know the plated weight and what is left after racking and driver, and treat a roadside stop as a check of whether you did those two things, because that is exactly what it is. The fixed penalties are modest, at £50 to £300. The prohibition, the points and the ten day loss of the van are what actually cost money.

If you are buying a van: an MOT pass months earlier than it needed to be is a question, not a reassurance. Ask why, ask for the removal notice or the invoices, and read the advisory pattern for signs the van spent its life over its plated weight. The free MOT history check shows the whole trail in seconds and costs nothing, which is the right price for the first question you should ask about any working van.

Figures checked 10 September 2026. Fixed penalty levels are from the Fixed Penalty Order 2000 (SI 2000/2792), Schedule 1 item 27 and Schedule 2 table 5, as amended by the Fixed Penalty (Amendment) Order 2013 (SI 2013/1569) with effect from 16 August 2013. Roadside procedure, prohibition types, repair windows, deposit amounts and the full inspection rule are from the GOV.UK guide Roadside checks for HGV, van, bus or coach drivers, updated 2 September 2026. The walkaround items and the three points per tyre line are from the DVSA guidance Carry out van daily walkaround checks, published 8 October 2013. Weight definitions are from GOV.UK Vehicle weights explained. The 2024 to 2025 prosecution counts are DVSA enforcement data as analysed by Tempcover and reported by PHAM News on 11 August 2026. The illustrative payload arithmetic is ours and should be checked against the plate on any specific van.

title: Diesel DPF and Emissions MOT Failures: What Fails, What It Costs, and How to Read a Diesel Car or Van's MOT History
desc: What the MOT emissions test does to a diesel car or van, the smoke limits by age, the DPF removal fines, 2026 repair costs from £85 to £3,500, and how to spot DPF trouble in the free MOT history before you buy.
body:
Emissions is the part of the MOT that diesel owners fear and used car buyers ignore, and both have it the wrong way round. For an owner it is one of the easiest sections to pass, producing fewer defects in the DVSA data than lamps, suspension, brakes, tyres or wipers. For a buyer, an emissions entry in a diesel's MOT history is the most expensive line the record can contain, because the part behind it is a particulate filter that costs four figures to replace. This guide covers what the tester does to a diesel car or van, the smoke limits by age, the DPF rules and fines, what each fix costs in 2026, and how to read a diesel's record on the free MOT history checker before you hand over money.

  • The diesel MOT emissions test is a smoke opacity test with a meter in the tailpipe, plus a visual check that the emissions equipment is still fitted, plus a check of the engine warning light on diesels first used from 1 July 2008.
  • The default smoke limits are 3.0 or 2.5 per metre for diesels first used before July 2008, 1.5 from July 2008 to December 2013, and 0.7 from January 2014, unless the manufacturer's plate gives a lower figure.
  • Any visible smoke from a diesel fitted with a DPF is a major defect since 20 May 2018, whatever the meter says.
  • A removed or tampered DPF fails the test and, on the road, carries a fine of up to £1,000 for a car and £2,500 for a van, on DVSA's own figures.
  • Noise, emissions and leaks together caused 3.08 percent of cars and vans to fail in 2025 to 2026, almost all of it major rather than dangerous. Rare, but expensive.
  • A forced regeneration costs £85 to £100 and a DPF replacement £1,000 to £3,500 plus VAT in 2026, so the same MOT failure can cost £85 or £3,500 depending on what is actually wrong.

What the tester actually does to a diesel

The DVSA inspection manual for cars and light vans, section 8.2.2, sets out three separate checks on a diesel, and they are worth keeping apart because they fail for different reasons and cost different amounts to fix.

The first is a visual check of the emission control equipment: the oxidation catalyst, the particulate filter, the EGR valve and the SCR system, if fitted. The tester only inspects what is visible and identifiable. Anything missing, obviously modified or obviously defective is a major defect. The manual adds a DPF specific rule: a filter that has clearly been cut open and welded back up is rejected unless you can show a valid reason, such as cleaning.

The second is the engine malfunction indicator lamp, the amber engine symbol most people call the engine management light. On a diesel first used on or after 1 July 2008 the tester turns the ignition on and checks that the lamp lights and then goes out. If it stays on, or never lights, that is a major defect. Since 20 May 2018 this has been the commonest way a diesel fails on emissions without a wisp of smoke, because a blocked DPF, a failed pressure sensor, a stuck EGR valve or a lazy glow plug can all put the lamp on.

The third is the opacity test. On any diesel first used from 1980 the tester warms the engine to at least 80 degrees, purges it at around 2,500rpm for 30 seconds, runs it to its governed maximum, then fits the smoke meter and does a series of full throttle accelerations from idle. The car passes if the first reading is 60 percent of the limit or lower, or if the average of three readings is at or under the limit. A vehicle with a DPF must also show no visible smoke at all during the metered check. Hybrids, including mild hybrids, are not smoke tested.

Diesel first usedDefault smoke limitWhere it comes from
Before 1 July 2008, non turbo2.5 per metreInspection manual 8.2.2.2
Before 1 July 2008, turbocharged3.0 per metreInspection manual 8.2.2.2

1 January 2014 onwards0.7 per metreInspection manual 8.2.2.2
Any age, with a plate valueThe plate value plus 0.05Inspection manual 8.2.2.2, tolerance added to stop false failures
Any age, fitted with a DPFNo visible smoke of any colourDefect 8.2.2.2 (d), major, since 20 May 2018

Many manufacturers stamp a smoke limit on the VIN plate or an under bonnet sticker, sometimes as low as 0.01, and the tester must use that figure plus a 0.05 tolerance rather than the age default. A Euro 6 diesel in good health usually reads so low that the meter cannot register it, and the manual has a procedure for recording a pass when that happens.

The DPF rules, and the fine for removing one

Diesel particulate filters became effectively universal with Euro 5, which applied to all new cars from January 2011, and many Euro 4 diesels from the mid 2000s had them too. A DPF traps soot and burns it off when the exhaust gets hot enough, which on most cars means a sustained run at motorway speed. Short urban trips never get it there, the soot builds up, and the car eventually puts the warning light on and drops into reduced power. It is a driving pattern problem before it is a mechanical one.

Because the fix people were sold for years was to cut the filter out and remap the engine, DVSA added a specific DPF check to the MOT in February 2014. Its Matters of Testing blog, in a September 2017 post about a DPF removal business whose directors turned out to be MOT testers, states the penalties plainly: driving with the filter removed carries a fine of up to £1,000 for a car or £2,500 for a light goods vehicle. Since 2018 the manual has gone further, and evidence of tampering is a major defect in its own right, as is any visible smoke from a DPF equipped vehicle.

Two consequences for a buyer. A diesel from 2011 or later that smokes at all has either a broken DPF or no DPF, and both are a fail. And a diesel that has been "DPF deleted", which sellers occasionally admit to in adverts as if it were an upgrade, cannot legally be driven, will fail its next MOT if the tester spots it, and is likely to invalidate the insurance. There is no price at which that is a good buy.

How often diesels actually fail on emissions

The DVSA MOT testing data for Great Britain, class 3 and 4 initial failures by defect category, gives the honest scale of the problem. In the 2025 to 2026 financial year, noise, emissions and leaks defects appeared in 3.08 percent of tests and made up 5.89 percent of all defects found. Of that, 3.07 percent of tests was major and 0.03 percent dangerous. Set against the overall initial failure rate of 27.51 percent, emissions is a minor contributor. Lamps, at 10.44 percent of tests, suspension at 8.90, tyres at 6.23 and brakes at 6.10 all fail far more cars.

The figure covers petrol and diesel together and has drifted down over a decade, from 4.60 percent of tests under the old fuel and exhaust heading in 2013 to 2014, though DVSA re-cut the categories in 2018 so the two are not perfectly comparable. A well maintained diesel is not at any special risk of failing on emissions. What the data cannot show is the cost: a lamp failure is a £5 bulb, an emissions failure on a diesel is anything from an hour on a diagnostic laptop to a new filter. That asymmetry is why an emissions line deserves more attention than its 3 percent frequency suggests.

What each fix costs in 2026

These are typical independent garage figures from the Checkatrade DPF cleaning cost guide, updated June 2026, and the Bumper catalytic converter guide for 2026. Main dealer prices run 40 to 60 percent higher. Treat them as ranges to test a quote against, not quotes.

Severely blocked DPF, removed and cleaned off the carUp to £300, some specialists £250 to £500Several hours to a dayCheckatrade, June 2026

Emissions is not on the list of items that get a free retest after you take the car away, so expect a partial retest fee if you fix it elsewhere, and the full fee after 10 working daysGOV.UK, Getting an MOT: retest after a repair

The gap between the top and bottom of that table is the whole point. A diesel that failed on the warning light and passed the next day almost certainly had a forced regeneration or a sensor, not a new filter. A diesel that failed on smoke and passed three weeks later at a different station may have had £1,000 spent on it, or may have had the filter hollowed out. The MOT record shows the dates and the wording; it is up to you to ask which.

Reading a diesel's MOT history for emissions trouble

The DVSA record that the free checker shows carries the tester's defect wording and the manual reference for every fail and advisory. On emissions the entries you will see are drawn from a short list, and each one tells you something different.

Wording in the MOT historyManual referenceWhat it usually means on a dieselWhat to ask the seller
Engine MIL inoperative or indicating a malfunction8.2.2.2 (g)A stored fault code. Could be a £30 sensor or a blocked DPF. Most common diesel emissions fail since 2018.What was the fault code, and what was replaced. A garage invoice, not a verbal answer.
Exhaust on a vehicle fitted with a diesel particulate filter emits visible smoke of any colour8.2.2.2 (d)The filter is cracked, blocked past recovery, or gone. This is the expensive one.Invoice for the filter or the off car clean. If the pass came from a different station days later, ask why.
Smoke opacity levels exceed the manufacturer's specified limit, or the default limit8.2.2.2 (a) or (b)On a pre 2011 diesel without a DPF, often worn injectors, turbo seals or a tired engine. On a DPF car, see the row above.What was the smoke reading before and after. The garage keeps the printout for three months.
Emission control equipment fitted by the manufacturer missing, obviously modified or obviously defective, or evidence that the DPF has been tampered with8.2.2.1 (a) or (c)The filter or EGR has been removed or gutted. Walk away unless there is an invoice for a new filter.Nothing. This is a car to leave.
Emissions test unable to be completed8.2.2.2 (e)Often an engine the tester judged unsafe to rev: low oil, a noise, a doubtful cambelt. Not an emissions problem, a general condition warning.What stopped the test, and what has been done since.

Then look at the shape of the whole record, not just the emissions lines. A diesel with very low annual mileage, under about 6,000 a year, on a DPF equipped car is a soot builder by definition; that pattern of short trips is what blocks filters, and the MOT history gives you the annual mileage on every test. A diesel that failed on the warning light two years in a row has a fault someone keeps clearing rather than fixing. A diesel whose pass came the same day as its fail, on emissions only, probably had a forced regeneration in the car park, which is a legitimate fix for a light blockage and a temporary one for a heavy one. The scorecard flags repeat failures and mileage patterns automatically, and the advisories guide covers how to read the rest of the advisory pattern.

Vans: the same test, a bigger fine, and a worse driving pattern

A diesel van up to 3,500kg is tested to exactly the same section of the manual as a car. Three things are different. The fine for a removed DPF is £2,500 rather than £1,000. The typical van working day, a hundred short stops with the engine barely warm between them, is the worst possible duty cycle for a particulate filter, which is why delivery vans block DPFs far more often than a commuter car. And a van is usually bought by someone who cannot afford a week off the road, so a £3,500 filter is a business problem rather than an annoyance.

If you are buying a used van, read the emissions lines alongside the load related advisories in our used van MOT history guide, and be more suspicious, not less, of a van with ten years of urban work and not one emissions entry. Either it has been driven on long runs, which the mileage will show, or the filter has been dealt with in a way that does not appear on paper.

What you do not need to pay for

You do not need a pre MOT emissions test. If the warning light is off and the car does not smoke, it will pass, and a garage charging for a separate smoke test beforehand is charging for the same test twice. You do not need fuel additives sold as DPF cleaners to pass; DVSA measures smoke, not soot loading, and a filter blocked enough to smoke needs a regeneration or a clean, not a bottle. And you do not need a DPF delete to solve a DPF problem. It is illegal, it fails the test, and the legal fix, an hour of forced regeneration at £85 to £100, is usually enough if the light has only just come on.

What is worth doing on a diesel you own: one proper run of 20 minutes or more at sustained speed every couple of weeks, and acting on the DPF light the week it appears rather than the week before the MOT. Ignoring it is what turns an £85 clean into a four figure replacement.

Plain verdict

If you own a diesel: the emissions test is not the thing to worry about. Keep the warning light off, give the car a long run now and then, and it will pass. If you are buying a diesel car or van from 2011 onwards: the emissions lines in the MOT history are the most expensive lines on the page, read every one, and ask for the invoice behind any fail that turned into a pass. If the record shows the DPF has been removed or tampered with, or the seller tells you it has, the answer is no at any price. The free MOT history check shows every emissions entry with the tester's wording and the manual reference, which is everything in this guide applied to the exact vehicle in front of you.

The February 2014 DPF check and the £1,000 and £2,500 fines are from the DVSA Matters of Testing blog, 25 September 2017. Failure rates are from the DVSA MOT testing data for Great Britain, class 3 and 4 initial failures by defect category, 2025 to 2026 full year. Repair costs are from the Checkatrade DPF cleaning cost guide updated June 2026 and the Bumper catalytic converter replacement cost guide for 2026, and are typical independent garage ranges excluding VAT. Retest rules are from GOV.UK. The reading of MOT history patterns is our own and should be checked against the specific record.

title: Loud Exhausts, LED Bulbs, Tail Tidies and Small Plates: Which Motorcycle Modifications Fail the MOT in 2026
desc: What the DVSA motorcycle manual actually says about aftermarket exhausts, NOT FOR ROAD USE cans, LED headlamp bulbs, tail tidy indicators and number plates, what the roadside law says instead, and how a modified bike shows up in the MOT record. Free MOT history checks for cars, vans, motorcycles and lorries.
body:
A loud can, an LED bulb, a tail tidy and a small plate are the four most common changes made to a used motorcycle in the UK, and each one is judged by two different rulebooks. The MOT tester works from the DVSA inspection manual for motorcycles, last updated on 1 April 2026. A police officer works from the Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations 1986. They do not agree, which is why a bike can pass its MOT on Monday and be stopped on Tuesday. This guide sets out what each says, and what a buyer can read off the free MOT history before viewing. The checker on this site covers cars, vans, motorcycles and lorries.

The short version

  • The MOT noise check is a judgement, not a measurement. The tester warms the engine, revs it to about half maximum and fails it only if it is clearly unreasonably louder than a standard bike. No decibel meter is used.
  • A silencer stamped NOT FOR ROAD USE, TRACK USE ONLY or similar is a Major fail on its own, however quiet it is. That is manual section 6.1.2(c).
  • There is no emissions test in a motorcycle MOT at all. Section 3 of the manual is marked not in use and section 8 covers noise only.
  • The car manual fails a halogen headlamp converted to LED or HID. The motorcycle manual does not contain that rule. A bike headlamp is judged on colour, intensity and aim.
  • A motorcycle registered on or after 1 September 2001 must only display a rear plate. Plates fitted after 1 September 2021 must carry BS AU 145e and use a single shade of black. The tester rejects only what is obviously wrong. The roadside fine is up to £1,000.
  • Mirrors are not inspected in a motorcycle MOT.
  • A modification shows up in the MOT record as a defect line with a manual reference. A noise fail followed by a pass the next day is the footprint of a can swapped for the test.

Two rulebooks, and passing one does not satisfy the other

The MOT answers one question: on the day of the test, did the bike meet the minimum standard in the manual. The manual is deliberately narrow and says nothing about anything outside its list. Construction and Use says what a vehicle must be like every time it is on a road, and it is enforced by police and DVSA officers, not testers. So an exhaust can pass section 8 of the manual and still be an offence under regulation 57B. Where this guide says "passes", it means the MOT and nothing more.

Exhausts: the noise test, the marking rule and the baffle question

Section 8.1.1 of the motorcycle manual is short. The tester should assess the noise by revving a warm engine to approximately half its maximum speed, and the system should be in such condition, or of such a type, that the noise is not clearly unreasonably above the level expected from a similar motorcycle with a standard silencer in average condition. The defect, noise levels in excess of those permitted, is Major. There is no figure, no meter and no test track. It is one person's ear against their memory of the standard bike, and on a twist and go scooter the tester cannot rev the engine at all.

A well made road legal aftermarket system will usually pass. A race can with the baffle removed usually will not, and a tester who is unsure tends to fail rather than pass, because their own licence is on the line. The one thing that is not subjective is section 6.1.2(c): a silencer marked NOT FOR ROAD USE, TRACK USE ONLY or similar words is a Major fail regardless of how it sounds. Race cans are stamped that way because they were never put through noise approval, so the marking does the tester's job for them. The removable baffle itself is not a defect. A can with the baffle in and no track marking is tested as it stands. What the manual cannot see is that the baffle comes out again in the car park, and that is what the roadside rules are for.

Under regulation 57A, a replacement silencer on a bike first used on or after 1 January 1985 must be built and marked to the relevant standard, in practice the British Standard or EU approval mark cast into the can. Regulation 57B makes it an offence to use a bike altered so that it is materially louder than it would be in standard working order, and regulation 97 bans avoidable excessive noise from any vehicle. These are Construction and Use offences under section 42 of the Road Traffic Act 1988: a £50 non-endorsable fixed penalty under the Fixed Penalty Order 2000 as amended in 2013, or up to £1,000 in court. No points, but a rectification notice and a second stop can follow.

Headlamps, indicators, the plate lamp and the reflector

Here the motorcycle manual is more lenient than the car manual, and most advice online is written for cars. The car manual, section 4.1.4, says halogen headlamp units on vehicles first used on or after 1 April 1986 must not be converted to HID or LED bulbs, and a converted unit must be failed for light source and lamp not compatible. The motorcycle manual has no equivalent sentence. Its section 4.1.4 requires white, yellow or mainly white with a blue tinge, intensity not significantly reduced, and defines a light source as any bulb, LED or other means of emitting light. Section 4.1.2 then requires the dipped beam cut off between 0.5 and 2.75 percent below horizontal for a lamp centred at 850mm or less from the ground, with the kick up visible. So an LED bulb in a halogen reflector is not an automatic fail on a bike. It passes only if the beam is still a proper European dip the tester can aim, and a cheap bulb in a reflector built for a filament usually scatters light above the cut off and fails on aim instead. For a buyer, a headlamp aim fail after a clean pass the year before is often a bulb change, not a fork problem.

Indicators are where tail tidy kits fail. Section 4.4.3 requires amber light and a minimum separation between the illuminating surfaces of 240mm at the front and 180mm at the rear on a solo motorcycle, 240mm and 160mm on a moped, and 400mm at both ends with a sidecar. The tester does not measure and rejects only what is obviously wrong, but micro indicators tucked under a shortened tail often are. Flash rate must be 60 to 120 per minute; a fast flash after fitting LEDs is Minor, recorded but not a fail. Sequential indicators are expressly not a reason to fail.

Two more things go missing with a tail tidy. The rear plate must be lit whenever the position lamps are on, so a plate lamp wired out is a Major fail under 4.7.1(b)(ii) if it was the only one. And the manual requires one red rear reflector on the centre line and says in terms that reflective tape is not an acceptable substitute. Plenty of tidies ship with a sticker where the reflector used to be. It does not count.

Number plates: what the tester checks and what the officer checks

The tester inspects the rear plate only. Under section 0.1, a plate must not be obscured, damaged or delaminated, must not have background overprinting or tints and films over the characters, and on a bike first registered on or after 1 September 2001 must not have a honeycomb background. Characters must be the right size, stroke and spacing, in the prescribed font or substantially similar, not italic or broken. Rear plates on motorcycles must be two lines, with three lines and larger 89mm characters allowed only on bikes first used before 1 September 2001. On a plate fitted on or after 1 September 2021 every character must be a single shade of black, so two tone and carbon effect characters are out. Imported bikes with no room for a standard plate can carry a smaller one. The tester does not measure and rejects only what is obviously incorrect. All four plate defects are Major.

GOV.UK adds the roadside side. A motorcycle registered on or after 1 September 2001 must display a plate at the rear only; older bikes may carry a front plate but do not have to. A plate fitted after 1 September 2021 must be marked BS AU 145e and show the supplier. The penalty for an incorrectly displayed plate is up to £1,000, on top of the MOT fail. A small plate is the modification most likely to be let through by a tester who is not obviously bothered and then picked up by an officer who is.

What the MOT does not police on a bike

Two absences surprise people. First, there is no emissions test in a motorcycle MOT. The car manual has a full section on exhaust emissions with metered limits. The motorcycle manual has section 3 marked "not in use" and section 8 covering noise only. A decat pipe or a remap is invisible to the test. Second, mirrors are not inspected. The motorcycle manual has no mirror section, so bar end mirrors, one mirror or none at all make no difference to the certificate. Neither absence makes the modification lawful or sensible. It just means the MOT is not where it will be caught. For the longer list of things the test never looks at, including engine, clutch and service condition, read what the DVSA data says really fails a bike.

One table: the modification, the MOT outcome, the roadside position

ModificationMOT outcome (motorcycle manual, April 2026)Roadside position
Aftermarket road legal can, marked, baffle inPasses if not clearly louder than standard (8.1.1)Lawful if marked to standard under reg 57A
Same can, baffle outMajor if clearly too loud at the testOffence under reg 57B, £50 fixed penalty, up to £1,000 in court
Race can stamped NOT FOR ROAD USEMajor on the marking alone (6.1.2(c))Not marked to standard, offence under reg 57A
LED bulb in halogen headlampNot an automatic fail on a bike; must give correct colour and aim (4.1.2, 4.1.4)Depends on the lamp still meeting lighting regulations
Micro indicators on a tail tidyMajor if separation obviously under 180mm rear or 240mm front (4.4.3)Same separation rule applies
Fast flash after LED indicatorsMinor only (4.4.4)Rarely enforced alone
Reflector replaced with tapeFail; tape is expressly not acceptable (4.8)Mandatory reflector still required
Small or show plateMajor only if obviously wrong (0.1)Fine up to £1,000, GOV.UK
Decat, remap, mirrors removedNot inspectedNot an MOT matter; other rules may apply

What a modified bike leaves in the MOT record

This is the part only a history checker can show you. Every defect is recorded in the manual's own wording with its section number, and it stays on the public record. A line reading "Exhaust noise levels in excess of those permitted (8.1.1 (a))" tells you the bike was presented with a loud can. "Number plate does not conform to the specified requirements (0.1 (d))" tells you about the plate. "Headlamp emitted colour or intensity not in accordance with the requirements (4.1.4 (a))" is very often a bulb. Testers also add free text advisories, and "exhaust modified" appears more often than sellers would like.

The pattern to look for is the fail and the fast pass. A Major on noise, then a pass on the same or the following day with nothing else changed, means the standard can went back on for the retest. The retest is free if the bike is left at the station and retested within ten working days, so this costs the seller nothing and is routine. It does not make the bike a bad buy. It does tell you that "road legal exhaust" in the advert needs testing with your own ears, and that you should ask whether the original can is included. The reverse matters too: a bike with a clean record and a race can in the photos has probably never been tested with it fitted, so the certificate says nothing about how loud it is.

Run the registration on the free MOT history check, read the defect wording section by section, then read how to read the gaps in a bike's record, because a modified bike is often also a summer only bike and the two patterns overlap. The buyer scorecard counts repeated advisories for you.

The verdict

An MOT pass tells you the tester did not think the bike was clearly louder than standard on the day, found no track marking, could aim the headlamp, and saw nothing obviously wrong with the plate and the indicators. It does not tell you the bike is lawful on the road, because the MOT does not measure noise, does not test emissions, does not look at mirrors and does not get a ruler out for the plate. If you own a modified bike, the cheap fixes are the ones that actually get caught: put a real reflector back, wire the plate lamp in, fit a two line plate to BS AU 145e, and keep the standard can. If you are buying, read the defect lines with the section numbers and trust the pattern over the advert. Most of the time the modifications are harmless and the paperwork is fine. When it is not, the record usually says so.

Sources: DVSA MOT inspection manual for motorcycles, sections 0.1, 4.1, 4.4, 4.7, 4.8, 6.1.2 and 8.1.1, updated 1 April 2026; DVSA MOT inspection manual for cars and passenger vehicles, section 4.1.4; Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations 1986, regulations 57, 57A, 57B and 97, legislation.gov.uk; GOV.UK, Displaying number plates; Road Traffic Act 1988 section 42; Fixed Penalty Order 2000 as amended 2013. Figures checked 11 September 2026.
