title: MOT brake failure: what each defect actually costs to fix on a car or van
desc: Brakes are the most common dangerous MOT fail on UK cars and vans. What each brake defect line means, what it costs to put right in 2026, and how to read it in a used vehicle's MOT history.
body:
A brake failure on an MOT is the one that stops you driving away. This guide covers cars and vans tested in classes 4 and 7, with a note on where motorcycles differ. In summary:

  • Brakes failed 6.10 percent of all car and van MOT tests in the 2025 to 2026 year, but they were 28.80 percent of all dangerous defects. Only tyres beat them.
  • A pad worn to its indicator is a Major. A pad below 1.5mm is Dangerous, and a Dangerous fail means the vehicle cannot legally be driven away, even for repair.
  • Pads and discs on one axle cost roughly £185 to £240 at an independent garage on the April 2026 Checkatrade figures. Pads alone are £100 to £135.
  • Corroded brake pipes, the classic fail on a ten year old car, are £75 to £180 a pipe. A handbrake cable is £120 to £340 fitted.
  • Brakes are not on the free next day retest list. If you take the vehicle away and bring it back within ten working days you can be charged a partial retest fee. Leave it at the test centre and the retest is free.
  • In a used vehicle's MOT history, a brake efficiency fail followed by a same day pass usually means new pads or a cleaned up disc. A pipe corrosion fail is worth more attention, because the pipe next to it is the same age.

How often brakes actually fail

The DVSA publishes initial failure figures by defect category every quarter. For class 3 and 4 vehicles, which is cars and small vans, the full 2025 to 2026 year (April 2025 to March 2026, published 10 September 2026) looks like this.

Defect categoryShare of tests failedShare of all defectsShare of dangerous defects
Lamps, reflectors and electrical10.44%24.89%1.27%
Suspension8.90%20.49%5.32%
Tyres6.23%12.94%60.60%
Brakes6.10%15.18%28.80%
Visibility4.28%7.72%0.10%
Noise, emissions and leaks3.08%5.89%0.26%
Overall initial failure rate27.51%7.22% of tests had a dangerous item

Read the last column. Lamps fail more tests than anything else, but almost none of those fails are dangerous. Brakes and tyres between them account for nearly nine in ten of every Dangerous defect recorded. That matters because the category on the defect line decides whether you can drive home. A Major fail can be driven to a repairer or a pre booked test if the old certificate is still in date. A Dangerous fail cannot be driven at all, and the penalty for doing so is up to £2,500, three points and a possible ban.

Vans fail more often across the board. Class 7 vans (3,000kg to 3,500kg) had a 34.00 percent initial failure rate in the same year against 27.51 percent for cars, on 1,107,819 tests. Brake wear on a van that spends its life loaded is faster than on a car, which is why brake lines are worth reading closely in a used van's MOT history.

What the tester is actually checking

Section 1 of the DVSA inspection manual for cars and light commercials (last updated 1 June 2026) covers brakes. There are two halves. The first is a visual and physical inspection of the parts: pedal, servo, master cylinder, pipes, hoses, pads, discs, drums, callipers, the parking brake lever or switch, and warning lamps. The second is a performance test on a roller brake tester, where each wheel's braking effort is measured and the software works out efficiency and imbalance.

The efficiency requirements are fixed numbers. A car first used on or after 1 September 2010 must achieve 58 percent service brake efficiency. A car first used before that date, and any van (N1), must achieve 50 percent. The parking brake must reach 16 percent on every vehicle except a handful of pre 1968 and pre 1915 categories. If more than half the wheels lock on the rollers, the efficiency requirement is treated as met without a calculation.

Imbalance is the one that catches people out. If one wheel on an axle produces less than 70 percent of the effort of the other wheel, that is a Major. On a steered axle, below 50 percent is Dangerous. A seized calliper slider or a corroded piston on one side is the usual cause, and the car will often feel fine to the driver.

Each brake defect line, what it means and what it costs

The wording on the MOT record follows the manual. The table below maps the common lines to the repair and to the 2026 price range. Pad and disc figures are Checkatrade's April 2026 averages for an independent garage. Pipe and cable figures are from Bumper's 2025 cost guides. Dealer prices run higher, and BMW and Mercedes pads and discs average £358 to £378 on the same Checkatrade data against £198 for a Toyota.

Defect line (manual reference)CategoryUsual repairTypical cost, 2026
Brake lining or pad worn down to wear indicator (1.1.13 a i)MajorPads on that axle£100 to £135
Brake lining or pad worn below 1.5mm (1.1.13 a ii)DangerousPads, and usually discs, because a pad that thin has scored them£185 to £240 per axle
Brake disc or drum significantly and obviously worn (1.1.14 a i)MajorDiscs and pads on that axle£185 to £240 per axle
Brake pipe damaged or excessively corroded (1.1.11 c)MajorNew pipe section, bleed£75 to £180 per pipe
Leaking brake pipe or connection on a hydraulic system (1.1.11 b ii)DangerousNew pipe or union, bleed, often more than one pipe£75 to £180 per pipe, more if several
Flexible brake hose excessively deteriorated (1.1.12)MajorNew hose, bleed£75 to £180 per hose
Service brake efficiency below minimum requirement (1.2.2 a i)MajorDepends on the cause, usually pads, discs or a sticking calliper£100 to £240 for pads or pads and discs, a calliper needs a quote
Brakes imbalance across an axle (1.2.1)Major, Dangerous if below 50% on a steered axleFree off or replace the calliper on the weak sideLabour only if freed off, a new calliper needs a quote
Parking brake efficiency below minimum requirement (1.4.2)MajorAdjustment, cable, or rear shoesAdjustment is labour only, cable £120 to £340
Parking brake inoperative on one side (1.4.1 a)MajorCable or seized rear mechanism£120 to £340

Two things the manual says that most garages will not tell you. A disc worn below the manufacturer's minimum thickness is not a fail on its own. The manual's words are that a disc "must be significantly worn before you should reject it", and being under the maker's limit "is not a reason in itself". So a garage quoting new discs because "they are under spec" is giving you a servicing recommendation, not an MOT requirement. The second is that an illuminated pad wear warning lamp is expressly not a reason for failure. The pad has to be physically worn to the indicator.

On brake pipes the manual asks the tester to reject when wall thickness is reduced by a third, about 0.25mm on a typical pipe, and admits this is not easy to judge. Where the tester is unsure, the instruction is to give the benefit of the doubt. So a pipe corrosion advisory one year and a fail the next is a tester who watched it get worse, not an inconsistency.

Retest rules: brakes are the expensive one

This is where a brake fail costs more than the parts. GOV.UK's retest page lists the items that get a free partial retest if the vehicle is brought back to the same station before the end of the next working day. Lamps, mirrors, wipers, plates, seat belts, wheels and tyres are all on it. Brakes are not. Neither is suspension, steering or anything in the emissions section.

So the choice on a brake fail is one of three. Leave the vehicle at the test centre, let them repair it, and the retest within ten working days is free. Take it away for repair elsewhere and bring it back within ten working days, and the station can charge a partial retest fee. Miss the ten working days and it is a full test again at up to £54.85 for a car or £58.60 for a class 7 van. The MOT cost guide has the full fee table.

If the fail is Dangerous, the take it away option is not really an option. The vehicle cannot be driven on the road, so it is either repaired on site or moved on a trailer or recovery truck, and that cost comes on top.

Reading brake lines in a used car or van's MOT history

The MOT record shows every defect, its category and the date, so brake history is one of the few parts of a car's past you can actually verify before buying. Run the registration through the free MOT history check and look at the brake lines in this order.

A pad or disc fail followed by a pass the same day or the next day is the least worrying pattern on the list. It means the garage fitted pads, probably discs, and retested. The car left with new brakes. Ask for the invoice and the date will match.

A brake efficiency or imbalance fail followed by a fast pass is worth one question: what was done. A sticking calliper that was freed off with a wire brush and copper grease can stick again within a year. A replaced calliper will not.

A brake pipe corrosion fail, or a run of pipe corrosion advisories over two or three years, tells you about the underside of the car, not just the pipe. Brake pipes corrode in the same conditions as sills, subframes and fuel lines. If one pipe has been replaced, the ones either side of it are the same age and have lived in the same salt. Budget for the rest, or look underneath before you pay.

Repeated parking brake fails, especially on a car with a manual lever, usually mean seized rear callipers or a cable that has been adjusted to its limit. It is cheap to fix but it is also a sign the car has sat for long periods, which is worth cross checking against the mileage between tests.

Advisories on brakes are covered in more detail in the advisories guide. The short version is that "brake pads wearing thin" as an advisory on the last pass is a £100 to £135 job you will be doing within a few months, and you should price it into the offer.

A note on motorcycles

Motorcycle brakes are tested under a separate manual and a separate defect category, and the numbers above do not apply. The class 1 and 2 data shows a very different picture, with lamps alone at more than 40 percent of all defects. The motorcycle MOT guide has the bike specific figures.

Verdict

A brake fail is not the expensive fail people assume it is. Pads and discs on one axle are a £185 to £240 job on a normal car, and pads alone are around £100 to £135. What makes brakes costly is the retest rule, because they are not on the free next day list, and the Dangerous category, because a pad under 1.5mm or a leaking pipe means the car goes nowhere under its own power until it is fixed.

For a buyer, brake lines in the MOT record are useful precisely because they are cheap to fix. A seller who has let a Dangerous brake defect happen, or who has a three year run of pipe corrosion advisories with no repair, has told you how the rest of the car has been looked after. That is worth more than the £200 you would spend on new pads.

Figures in this guide: DVSA MOT testing data for Great Britain, class 3 and 4 initial failures by defect category, 2025 to 2026 total, published 10 September 2026. DVSA MOT inspection manual for private passenger and light commercial vehicles, section 1, updated 1 June 2026. GOV.UK retest after a repair page. Checkatrade brake pad replacement cost guide, updated April 2026. Bumper brake pipe (March 2025) and handbrake cable (October 2025) cost guides.

title: Suspension MOT failure on a van or car: what springs, shocks, bushes and ball joints cost to fix
desc: Suspension is the biggest single MOT defect group on UK cars and vans. What each suspension fail line means, what a spring, shock absorber, bush or ball joint costs to put right in 2026, and how to read suspension advisories in a used van's MOT history.
body:
Suspension is the fail that surprises people. It rarely makes a noise you would notice on a loaded van, it rarely lights a warning lamp, and it is the largest single group of defects the DVSA records on cars and vans. This guide is written for van owners and small fleets first, because vans carry weight every day and wear suspension faster, but every figure for cars and light vans in classes 3 and 4 is here too. In summary:

  • Suspension defects were found on 8.90 percent of all car and small van MOT tests in the 2025 to 2026 year, and made up 20.49 percent of every defect recorded. No other category is bigger.
  • On class 7 vans, the 3,000kg to 3,500kg group, suspension was on 8.43 percent of tests and 13.73 percent of defects, behind lamps and brakes. The overall class 7 failure rate is 34.00 percent against 27.51 percent for cars.
  • A broken coil spring costs roughly £167 to £275 an axle to replace on a car or small van on the Checkatrade figures. Shock absorbers average £379 a pair. A ball joint is £75 to £180 on a car and £155 to £311 on a full size Transit.
  • Most suspension fails are Major, not Dangerous. You can drive away and get it fixed. A fractured main leaf spring, a component about to detach, or a corroded mounting that affects control are the Dangerous ones.
  • Suspension is not on the free next day retest list. Leave the van at the test centre and the partial retest is free. Take it away and bring it back within ten working days and you can be charged a partial retest fee.
  • In a used van's MOT history, a suspension fail that clears the next day is normal wear. The same bush or spring advisory three years running is a van that has been driven on its fail line, not repaired.

How common suspension fails are, by vehicle class

The DVSA publishes initial failure figures by defect category for every MOT class. The table below is the full 2025 to 2026 year, published on 10 September 2026, which is the most recent complete year. "Percent of tests" is how many tests had at least one defect in that category. "Percent of defects" is that category's share of every defect written down.

Category, 2025 to 2026 full yearClass 3 and 4: cars and small vansClass 7: vans 3,000kg to 3,500kg
Suspension, percent of tests8.90 percent8.43 percent
Suspension, percent of all defects20.49 percent13.73 percent
Suspension, share of Dangerous defects5.32 percent7.08 percent
Lamps, percent of all defects24.89 percent30.58 percent
Brakes, percent of all defects15.18 percent22.38 percent
Overall initial failure rate27.51 percent34.00 percent
Tests in the year33,310,5341,107,819

Two things stand out. On cars and small vans, suspension is the biggest category there is, bigger than lamps once you look at share of defects rather than share of tests. On heavy vans the order changes: brakes and lamps come first, suspension third. That does not mean van suspension is better. It means heavy vans fail more of everything, 3.09 defects per failed test against 2.39 for cars, and brakes take a bigger share of a bigger total.

The Dangerous column is the reassuring one. Suspension is a small share of Dangerous defects on both classes. Tyres and brakes are nine in ten of every Dangerous line. Most suspension fails are Major, which means the vehicle failed but you can legally drive it to be repaired if the MOT has not already run out.

What the tester is actually checking

Section 5.3 of the DVSA inspection manual for cars and light commercial vehicles, updated 1 June 2026, covers springs, shock absorbers, arms and sub-frames, joints and bushes, air suspension, and the structure around every mounting. The tester jacks the vehicle so the springs are unloaded, then levers and rocks each wheel looking for play. On the front of most vans this is done with wheel play detectors, the plates that shake the wheel while the tester watches the joints.

The manual has fixed limits that garages rarely quote. Play in a spring pin or bush is excessive above 2mm on a 12mm pin, above 3mm on a 25mm pin, and above 10 percent of the diameter on anything bigger. A rubber bush is only rejected when the tester can see serious deterioration of the bonding or the rubber, not because it moves. Many bushes are designed to move. A MacPherson strut top mount is allowed to have lateral play when the suspension is hanging; it fails only when the play is wear.

Shock absorbers have one rule that saves money: slight seepage leaving a film of fluid on the body is not a fail. Severe leakage, negligible damping, or a worn bush is. A missing bump stop rubber is not a fail at all, whatever a garage tells you. And the tester is not allowed to fail a shock absorber for being missing unless one was fitted as standard.

The structural rule matters most on older vans. Any load bearing metal within 30cm of a spring, sub-frame or suspension mounting is a prescribed area. Corrosion there that significantly reduces strength is a Major fail, and if it is bad enough to affect control it is Dangerous. This is where a nine year old van that lives on gritted roads fails, and it is the one suspension line that can cost more than the van is worth.

Each suspension defect line, what it means and what it costs

The prices below are for an independent garage, parts and labour, from the sources named under each. Vans sit at the top of every range and often above it, because the parts are heavier and the job takes longer. Coil springs and shock absorbers are replaced in pairs across an axle.

Manual referenceWhat the fail sheet saysCategoryUsual repairRough cost, 2026
5.3.1 (b)(i)Spring or spring component fractured or seriously weakenedMajorPair of coil springs, one axleFront £175 to £275, rear £167 to £177 on a car (Checkatrade, table updated May 2024, page June 2025). A Transit rear leaf spring is £540 for the genuine part alone on Ford's own parts shop, before fitting.
5.3.1 (b)(ii)Spring main leaf fracturedDangerousLeaf spring, one side or bothAs above. Cannot be driven away.
5.3.2 (b)Shock absorber severely leaking or not functioningMajorPair of shock absorbers, one axle£150 to £500, average £379; front pair £416, rear pair £321 (Bumper, October 2025). Transit Custom front £240 to £455, full size Transit front £247 to £633 (Fixter, September 2026).
5.3.2 (c)Shock absorber bush excessively wornMajorBush, or the whole unit if the bush is not sold separately£60 to £120 labour an axle plus the part (Bumper labour figure).
5.3.3 (b)(i)Suspension component excessively damaged or corrodedMajorWishbone or arm, one sideVaries widely. A pressed steel wishbone with its bushes and ball joint is often £150 to £300 fitted on a car; van arms are more.
5.3.4 (a)(i)Suspension pin, bush, joint or bearing excessively wornMajorBall joint, drop link, or bushBall joint £75 to £180, average £90 (Bumper, July 2025); Transit lower ball joint £155 to £311 (Fixter). Anti-roll bar drop links £60 to £130 a pair (Bumper, April 2026). Anti-roll bar bushes around £80 to £180.
5.3.4 (b)(i)Suspension joint dust cover severely deterioratedMinorNothing, or a new bootA Minor is a pass. Under £50 if you replace the boot.
5.3.4 (b)(ii)Dust cover missing or no longer keeps dirt outMajorUsually the whole jointAs a ball joint.
5.3.6 (a)(i)Load bearing structure within 30cm of a mounting significantly reduced by corrosionMajorWelded repair to the prescribed areaNo published range. Small local repairs start around £150 to £300; a corroded rear spring hanger or sub-frame mount on a van can run past £1,000.

Some of these lines are cheap to argue with. A dust cover that is split but still keeping dirt out is a Minor and the vehicle passes. A shock absorber with a film of oil on it passes. If a garage quotes you for either as an MOT repair, the manual is on your side.

Two are not worth arguing with. A fractured coil spring is a Major fail on the day, and springs snap in cold weather and potholes without warning, so the second spring on the same axle is the same age and usually goes next. Replace the pair. And a corroded prescribed area needs a welder, not a wire brush, because the tester will look for the repair next year and the manual says an inadequate repair is the same Major fail.

Retest rules: suspension is not on the free list

GOV.UK's retest page lists the items you can have retested free the next working day after taking the vehicle away. It covers lamps, mirrors, wipers, seat belts, wheels and tyres, and a few dozen other quick fixes. Springs, shock absorbers, bushes, ball joints and structure are not on it.

So a suspension fail leaves two routes. Leave the van at the test centre for the repair and it gets a partial retest within ten working days for no fee. Take it away to your own garage and bring it back within ten working days and the test centre can charge a partial retest fee. Take longer than ten working days and it is a full test at the full price, up to £54.85 for a car or £58.60 for a class 7 van. Full details are in our guide to the MOT fee and when the retest is free.

The practical answer for a working van is to book the MOT with a garage that can do suspension work on site. A spring or a ball joint is a same day job almost anywhere. Leaving it there costs you a day of the van. Taking it away costs you a day plus a fee.

Reading suspension lines in a used van's MOT history

Every advisory and fail is in the free record when you check a registration on MOT Check UK, and suspension lines are the most useful ones for a van buyer because they show how the van was used and how it was looked after.

A suspension fail followed by a pass on the same day or the next is nothing. It is the normal life of a van. A spring or a shock absorber wore out, the garage fitted a new one, the record shows both events. Ask which side and check the invoice if you want, but do not walk away from it.

Look instead at repeated advisories. "Nearside rear coil spring corroded" as an advisory three years in a row means the owner read the advisory and drove on. That spring is now a fail waiting to happen and the offside one is the same age. "Front suspension arm pin or bush slightly worn" repeated year after year is the same story. Price the repair from the table above and take it off the offer.

Look hardest at anything that mentions corrosion near a mounting, "prescribed area", or "spring hanger". On a van past eight years old these are the lines that turn into a welding bill. If the record shows a fail for corrosion in a prescribed area and a pass a week later, ask to see the underside. A proper repair is plated and painted. A quick one is underseal over the hole.

Finally, put the suspension lines next to the mileage. A van doing 30,000 miles a year with one spring in five years has been serviced. A van doing 8,000 miles a year with shock absorbers, drop links, ball joints and two springs in three years has either been loaded past its plate or driven on farm tracks. Our guide to reading a used van's MOT trail covers the mileage side, and the buy scorecard counts a repeated advisory against the vehicle automatically.

A note on cars and motorcycles

Everything in the manual section above applies to cars, which are tested in the same class 4 as small vans. The difference is money. Car springs and shock absorbers sit at the bottom of every range in the table, and a car ball joint is a £90 job where a Transit's is £155 or more. If you are pricing the same advisory on a Fiesta and on a Transit, do not use the same number.

Motorcycles have their own manual and their own data. In the class 1 and 2 figures for the same year, suspension is a small category and lamps dominate. A leaking fork seal is the usual bike suspension fail and the rules for it are in our motorcycle MOT guide.

Verdict

Suspension is the fail you should expect on any van past its fifth birthday, and on most cars past their eighth. It is common, it is nearly always Major rather than Dangerous, and the common repairs are £150 to £450 an axle. Do not panic over one fail line in a record and do not pay a garage to fix a seeping damper or a split dust cover that the manual says is a pass.

What should change your offer on a used van is a pattern: the same advisory repeated, or any corrosion near a mounting. Those are the lines that turn into a four figure bill, and a seller who left them for three years has told you how the rest of the van was treated. The record is free, so read it before you drive to see the van.

title: Tyre MOT failures: what fails, what it costs to fix, and why it is the cheapest fail to clear (cars, vans and motorcycles)
desc: Tyres are 6 in 10 of every Dangerous MOT defect on UK cars and vans. What the tester checks, the 1.6mm rule, 2026 tyre prices, the free next-day retest, and how to read tyre lines in a used car's MOT record.
body:
A tyre fail is the most common way a car or van leaves an MOT with a Dangerous defect, and it is also the cheapest fail to put right. This guide covers cars and vans tested in classes 4 and 7, with a note on where motorcycles differ. In summary:

  • Tyres failed 6.23 percent of all car and van MOT tests in the 2025 to 2026 year, but they were 60.60 percent of all Dangerous defects. Brakes were the only other category that came close.
  • Tread below 1.6mm in the central three quarters is a Dangerous fail, not a Major one. A Dangerous fail means the vehicle cannot legally be driven away, even to a tyre shop.
  • A mid-range tyre fitted and balanced costs roughly £85 to £135 in 2026. A budget tyre is £45 to £70 plus balancing. One tyre, not four, is usually all the test needs.
  • Wheels and tyres are on the GOV.UK list of items that get a free partial retest if you return by the end of the next working day. Motorcycles are the one exception.
  • For a buyer, repeated "worn close to legal limit" advisories in a car's record say more about the seller than about the car. Check the pattern free at MOT Check UK.

How common a tyre fail is, and why the Dangerous share matters

DVSA publishes MOT results by defect category every three months. The full 2025 to 2026 year for class 3 and 4 vehicles (cars and light vans up to 3,000kg) was published on 10 September 2026, and the tyre line reads like this: 6.23 percent of tests had at least one tyre defect, tyres were 12.94 percent of all defects recorded, and 4.47 percent of all tests had a Dangerous tyre defect. That last number is the one that matters. Across every category, Dangerous defects appeared on 7.22 percent of tests, so tyres alone account for 60.60 percent of every Dangerous line written in the year.

Put another way, on 33.3 million class 3 and 4 tests, roughly 1.49 million cars and light vans were declared dangerous to drive because of a tyre. Suspension is a bigger defect group overall (8.90 percent of tests) and lamps are bigger still (10.44 percent), but almost all of those are Major. Tyres are the category where the fail is most likely to be the serious kind.

Class, 2025 to 2026 full yearTests with a tyre defectTyres as share of all Dangerous defectsOverall initial failure rate
Classes 3 and 4 (cars, vans up to 3,000kg)6.23 percent60.60 percent27.51 percent
Class 7 (vans 3,000kg to 3,500kg)5.22 percent37.46 percent34.00 percent
Classes 1 and 2 (motorcycles)1.85 percent34.77 percent13.40 percent

Class 7 vans fail more often overall, but their tyre share of Dangerous defects is lower because brakes and steering take a larger slice on heavier vehicles. Motorcycles have few tyre fails in total, yet when a bike does get a Dangerous line, a third of the time it is a tyre.

What the tester actually checks

Section 5.2.3 of the DVSA inspection manual for cars and light commercial vehicles (updated 1 June 2026) lists the tyre defects and the category each one carries. Only the tyres fitted to the road wheels are inspected. A spare with a problem gets you a verbal warning, not a fail. The lines that produce most of the results in the MOT record are these.

Manual referenceDefect as it appears on the certificateCategory
5.2.3 (e)Tyre tread depth not in accordance with the requirementsDangerous
5.2.3 (d)(ii)Tyre has a lump, bulge or tear caused by separation or partial failure of its structure, or cords exposedDangerous
5.2.3 (j)Tyre valve seriously damaged or misaligned, likely to cause sudden deflationDangerous
5.2.3 (d)(i)Tyre has a cut deep enough to reach the ply or cordsMajor
5.2.3 (b)Tyres on the same axle are different sizesMajor
5.2.3 (c)Tyres on the same axle are of different structure (radial mixed with cross-ply)Major
5.2.3 (h)Tyre pressure monitoring system malfunctioning or obviously not workingMajor
5.2.3 (i)Tyre not fitted in compliance with the sidewall instructions (a directional tyre on backwards)Major
5.2.3 (f)Tyre fouling a part of the vehicle at the time of testMajor
5.2.3 (l)Tyre obviously under-inflatedMinor

Three things in the manual are worth knowing because garages rarely quote them. First, an asymmetric tyre fitted inside-out is not a fail. The tester should advise, and that is all. Second, a cut only fails if cord can be seen, or if a cut longer than 25mm or 10 percent of the section width lets the tester feel cord with a blunt tool. A surface cut with no cord showing passes. Third, there is no tyre age limit for cars, vans or motorcycles. The ten year rule introduced in February 2021 applies to the front steered axle of buses and coaches and to minibuses on single wheels. A twelve year old tyre on a low-mileage car passes if the tread and sidewall are sound, and it will usually collect a "cracking" or "perishing" advisory rather than a fail.

The TPMS line only applies to M1 passenger cars first used on or after 1 January 2012. A tyre pressure warning lamp that stays on because a tyre is simply low is not a fail on its own. A lamp that flashes and then stays on is the system telling the tester it has a fault, and that is the Major.

The 1.6mm rule, stated properly

For cars, vans up to 3,500kg and light trailers, the primary grooves of the tread must be at least 1.6mm deep across the central three quarters of the tread width and around the whole circumference. The outer quarter on each side can be completely bald and the tyre still passes. Only the primary grooves count, meaning the ones that carry the tread wear indicator bars. Shallow decorative sipes are ignored. Motorcycles, vehicles with more than eight passenger seats and lorries have a 1.0mm limit instead, and a moped only needs a visible pattern.

Because the limit is measured at the shallowest point anywhere round the tyre, a tyre that reads 2mm at the top can still fail if a flat spot or a worn inside edge takes one section below 1.6mm. Inside edge wear from bad alignment is the classic surprise fail: the tyre looks fine from outside the car and is bald where nobody looks.

What a Dangerous tyre fail actually means for you

The category changes what you can do next. A Major fail on an in-date MOT can be driven to a garage for repair. A Dangerous fail cannot. GOV.UK is plain that driving a vehicle in a dangerous condition carries a fine of up to £2,500, three penalty points and a possible ban, and that applies per tyre. A car with two bald tyres is six points. In practice a Dangerous tyre fail means the tyre is changed where the car stands, either by the test station or by a mobile fitter called to the forecourt.

This is also why tyres are the fail that most often leads to a same-day pass. Most test stations fit tyres, the job takes twenty to thirty minutes per wheel, and the retest is free. Compare that with a brake fail, where brakes are not on the free retest list and a car taken away for repair pays for a partial retest on return.

What it costs to fix in 2026

Tyre prices are set by size and brand tier far more than by the garage. The figures below are from the Checkatrade tyre change cost guide, last updated June 2026, and cover a standard car size fitted at a garage.

ItemTypical 2026 rangeSource
Budget tyre, supplied and fitted£45 to £70 per tyreCheckatrade, June 2026
Mid-range tyre, supplied and fitted£75 to £120 per tyreCheckatrade, June 2026
Premium tyre, supplied and fitted£220 to £1,200 per tyre (large wheels and performance cars at the top end)Checkatrade, June 2026
Wheel balancing£7 to £15 per wheelCheckatrade, June 2026
Puncture repair (tread area only)around £40Checkatrade, June 2026
Set of four winter tyres£600 to £800Checkatrade, June 2026
Partial retest for a tyre, returned next working day£0GOV.UK, retest after a repair

So the realistic bill for the most common tyre fail, one tyre below 1.6mm on a normal family car, is £85 to £135 for a mid-range tyre with balancing, or £55 to £85 on a budget tyre. A pair on the same axle is double that. Van tyres in 15 and 16 inch commercial sizes sit at the upper end of the mid-range band because of the higher load rating, and a class 7 van with two worn rears should budget £220 to £300.

The one cost that is easy to miss is alignment. If the tyre failed on inside-edge wear, fitting a new tyre without correcting the alignment means the new one wears the same way. Alignment is not part of the MOT and is not needed for the retest, but it is the difference between a tyre lasting the 20,000 to 30,000 miles Checkatrade quotes as normal and one that is back at the legal limit within the year.

The free retest rule, and how to use it

GOV.UK lists the items that qualify for a free partial retest if the vehicle goes back to the same test centre before the end of the next working day. "Wheels and tyres (excluding motorcycles and motorcycles with sidecar)" is on that list, and so is "tyre pressure monitoring system". That gives you three routes after a tyre fail.

  • Leave the vehicle at the test station, let them fit the tyre, retest free. Fastest, and fine if their tyre price is reasonable.
  • If the fail is Major rather than Dangerous (a cut, a mismatched size, a TPMS fault) and the old MOT is still in date, drive to a cheaper fitter, come back by the end of the next working day, retest free.
  • If the fail is Dangerous, have a mobile fitter come to the test station car park, then retest free the same day. You cannot drive it away on a Dangerous tyre, even to a tyre shop round the corner.

Come back between the second and the tenth working day and the station may charge a partial retest fee. After ten working days it is a full test at the full fee. Motorcycle tyres are the exception throughout: a bike tyre fail is either repaired on site or pays for a partial retest on return.

What you do not need to pay for

A tyre fail is where garages most often sell more than the test requires. The manual only requires tyres on the same axle to match in size and structure. It does not require them to match in brand, tread pattern or wear, and it says nothing at all about the other axle. Replacing one tyre is legal and passes the test. Four new tyres because one failed is a choice, not a requirement, although keeping a pair matched on the driven axle is sensible on any car and on all-wheel-drive cars it is usually specified by the maker.

You also do not need a premium tyre to pass. A budget tyre with 8mm of tread passes exactly as a £250 tyre does. Where premium tyres earn their money is wet braking and lifespan, which is a running cost decision rather than an MOT one. Part-worn tyres are legal but must have at least 2mm of tread and be marked "part worn", and you have no way of knowing how they were stored or how old they are. On a £50 saving that is a poor trade.

Finally, nitrogen inflation, tyre sealant top-ups and "tyre protection" plans do nothing for the test. Correct pressure, checked monthly, is the whole of the maintenance the MOT cares about.

Reading tyre lines in a used car's MOT record

For a buyer, the tyre section of an MOT history is less about the tyres, which the seller will usually have replaced, and more about how the car was run. Pull the record at MOT Check UK and look for these patterns.

  • "Tyre worn close to legal limit" appearing as an advisory at two or more consecutive tests: the owner ran tyres to the edge every year and probably treated servicing the same way. Read the rest of the advisories with that in mind.
  • A tread fail followed by a pass the same or next day: the cheapest fail there is, fixed immediately. Not a concern.
  • "Tyre slightly damaged/cracking or perishing" on a low-mileage car: the tyres are old, not worn. Check the date codes on the sidewall when you view it. Four tyres of the same age over eight years is £300 to £500 you should take off the price.
  • "Tyres on the same axle are different sizes" or "different structure": somebody fitted whatever was cheap or fitted the spare and left it on. Look for a matching pattern of odd repairs elsewhere in the record.
  • Inside-edge wear noted as an advisory more than once: the alignment was never fixed. Ask whether the car has been kerbed or in a collision, and look for suspension advisories at the same tests.
  • A TPMS fail on a 2012 or later car: ask for the invoice showing the sensor was replaced, and check the warning lamp goes out when you test drive.

If you are choosing between two cars, the side-by-side comparison puts both records next to each other so a pattern of tyre advisories on one and none on the other stands out straight away.

Plain verdict

A tyre fail is serious on the certificate and cheap on the invoice. It is the most likely reason a car or van is declared dangerous at its MOT, six in every ten Dangerous lines in 2025 to 2026, and yet one mid-range tyre fitted and balanced is around £100 and the retest is free if you sort it by the next working day. Fix the tyre that failed, fix the alignment if the wear was on one edge, and ignore anyone telling you the test requires four. For a buyer, a single tyre fail in a car's history means nothing. Repeated "close to the limit" advisories mean the seller ran the car to the wire, and that is worth knowing before you agree a price.

Figures in this guide: DVSA MOT testing data for Great Britain, initial failures by defect category for classes 1 and 2, 3 and 4, and 7, 2025 to 2026 total, published 10 September 2026, and MOT test results by class of vehicle for the same period. DVSA MOT inspection manual for private passenger and light commercial vehicles, section 5.2.3, updated 1 June 2026. GOV.UK pages "Getting an MOT: retest after a repair" and "Check your vehicle is safe to drive". Checkatrade tyre change cost guide, updated June 2026.

title: MOT lights failure: what bulbs, lamps and headlamp aim cost to fix on cars, vans and motorcycles
desc: Lamps are 24.89 percent of every MOT defect on UK cars and vans, the biggest category of all. What each lamp defect line means, what a bulb or a headlamp aim fix costs in 2026, why the retest is free for bulbs but not for aim, and how to read lamp lines in a used vehicle's MOT history.
body:
Lights are the single biggest source of MOT defects in Britain, on cars, on vans and on motorcycles. They are also, on a car, almost never dangerous and almost always cheap. This guide covers cars and light vans in classes 3 and 4, goods vehicles in class 7, and motorcycles in classes 1 and 2. In summary:

  • Lamps, reflectors and electrical equipment accounted for 24.89 percent of every defect recorded on a car or light van MOT in the 2025 to 2026 year, the largest category of the thirteen DVSA reports. Suspension was second at 20.49 percent and brakes third at 15.18 percent.
  • That is about 3.5 million tests out of 33.3 million with at least one lamps defect on the ticket.
  • On a car, lamps were only 1.27 percent of Dangerous defects. On a motorcycle they were 19.43 percent. The same category means two different things depending on what you ride or drive.
  • Most lamps items get a free partial retest if you return to the same station by the end of the next working day. Headlamp aim is written out of that list by name, and it is the expensive one.
  • For a buyer, a lamps line in a used vehicle record tells you nothing about the vehicle. A repeated headlamp aim failure might. Check the pattern free at MOT Check UK.

The biggest category nobody talks about

DVSA publishes MOT results by defect category every three months. The full 2025 to 2026 year for class 3 and 4 vehicles, meaning cars and light vans up to 3,000kg, was published on 10 September 2026. The lamps row reads like this.

MeasureLamps and electricalFor comparison
Share of all tests with at least one defect in this category10.44 percentSuspension 8.90, brakes 6.10, tyres 6.23
Share of all defects recorded24.89 percentSuspension 20.49, brakes 15.18, tyres 12.94
Share of all Major defects29.18 percentSuspension 23.25, brakes 12.71
Share of all Dangerous defects1.27 percentTyres 60.60, brakes 28.80

The overall initial failure rate for cars and light vans that year was 27.51 percent on 33,310,534 initial tests. Apply the 10.44 percent figure and roughly 3.5 million cars and vans picked up a lamps defect in twelve months.

The pattern is stable rather than a one year oddity. In April to June 2026, lamps were 9.98 percent of tests and 24.67 percent of defects, still the largest category. There is a mild autumn rise, 10.87 percent of tests in October to December 2025 against 10.36 percent in April to June 2025, with the same shape the year before. That is about half a percentage point, not the dramatic winter spike often claimed.

What actually fails, and what category it gets

Section 4 of the DVSA inspection manual covers lamps, reflectors and electrical equipment. Every defect carries a reference number, and that reference is what ends up on the certificate and in the MOT record. These are the lines that come up most.

Manual referenceDefectCategory
4.1.1 (a)(ii)Headlamp missing or inoperative, or more than half the LED sources outMajor
4.1.1 (a)(i)Up to half the LED sources in a headlamp not workingMinor
4.1.2 (a)Headlamp aim not within the limits in the requirementsMajor
4.1.2 (b)Headlamp aim unable to be testedMajor
4.1.4 (c)Light source and lamp not compatibleMajor
4.3.1 (a)(ii)A stop lamp missing or inoperativeMajor
4.3.1 (a)(iii)All stop lamps missing or inoperativeDangerous
4.4.1 (a)(ii)A direction indicator missing or inoperativeMajor
4.4.4 (a)Indicator flash rate not between 60 and 120 times a minuteMinor
4.5.1 (a)(ii)Obligatory rear fog lamp missing, or a fog lamp inoperativeMajor
4.6.1 (a)Reversing lamp inoperative, vehicles first used from 1 September 2009Major
4.7.1 (b)(i)One registration plate lamp out where two or more are fittedMinor
4.7.1 (b)(ii)The only registration plate lamp out, or all of them outMajor
4.8.1 (a)(ii)Reflector damaged over more than half its reflecting surfaceMajor
4.9.1 (a)(ii)Main beam or rear fog tell-tale missing or inoperativeMajor

Five rules in that section are worth knowing because garages rarely quote them.

  • All stop lamps out is the only Dangerous lamps line on a car. One brake light out is a Major. Both out, on a vehicle that has only two, is Dangerous, and that means it must not be driven away.
  • A single dead LED is usually a Minor. In a multiple light source lamp, up to half the sources out is Minor and more than half is Major. That covers headlamps, stop lamps, indicators and fog lamps.
  • Sequential indicators are expressly allowed. The manual states that indicators which function sequentially or dynamically are not a reason to fail.
  • Front fog lamps are only inspected on vehicles first used on or after 1 March 2018, and the same date applies to daytime running lamps, which are only inspected if fitted as original equipment. A front fog lamp with no wiring and no switch does not need to work, and where the tester is unsure the manual tells them to give the benefit of the doubt.
  • A registration plate lamp is a Minor if a second one still works. It becomes a Major only when it is the only one fitted, or all of them are out.

Headlamp aim, the one lamps fail that is not a bulb

Everything above is a bulb, a lens or a connector. Aim is different, and it is the part of section 4 that costs real money.

The tester puts the vehicle on a marked standing area, lines up beam setting equipment and reads the cut-off against a grid. For a European type dipped beam, the cut-off must sit between the 0.5 percent and 2.75 percent horizontal lines where the headlamp centre is 850mm or less from the ground, and between 1.25 percent and 2.75 percent where it is higher. The kick up to the left must be visible unless it has been masked or the lamp has a flat top pattern.

Two practical points come out of the manual. First, the tester must not carry out repairs during a test but is expressly allowed to make minor adjustments to headlamp aim, so on many cars this is a screwdriver turn at the bay and no fail at all. It pays to ask rather than assume. Second, where driver adjustable beam controls are fitted, the aim is checked at whatever setting the car arrived in, and only re-checked at the highest setting if it would otherwise fail for being too low. A dash dial left on 3 after a loaded trip can put a healthy headlamp outside the band.

Aim also fails when it cannot be measured. Reference 4.1.2 (b), "headlamp aim unable to be tested", is a Major, and a badly clouded lens or a scattered beam pattern from the wrong bulb lands there.

LED and HID conversions: the fail people do not see coming

Manual reference 4.1.4 is blunt about this. Existing halogen headlamp units on vehicles first used on or after 1 April 1986 must not be converted to use high intensity discharge or LED bulbs. If that conversion has been done, the headlamp must be failed for light source and lamp not compatible, a Major.

The distinction is unit versus bulb. A complete replacement headlamp unit manufactured with LED or HID light sources is fine and must not be failed on that reference, though it still has to meet everything else in section 4. Screwing an LED bulb into a reflector designed for a halogen filament is what fails, and it fails on the rule, not on how bright it looks. A bright white beam on a fifteen year old hatchback is usually a retrofit kit, and the MOT record will show it. The motorcycle manual carries no equivalent rule, which we covered in the guide on motorcycle exhaust and lighting modifications.

What it costs to put right in 2026

A bulb is the cheapest repair in the MOT. Bumper's headlight bulb cost guide, updated 19 September 2025, puts a halogen bulb at as little as £3 over the counter and £15 to £100 fitted, the spread depending almost entirely on how buried the lamp unit is, and reports Halfords charging roughly £8 to £15 for fitting, often free when the bulb is bought there.

JobTypical 2026 costNote
Halogen bulb, over the counter£5 to £30£3 at the bottom end for a basic H7
Halogen bulb bought and fitted£15 to £100Bumper range across all cars
Fitting labour, accessible unit£12 to £5015 to 30 minutes at £50 to £100 an hour
Fitting labour, bumper off job£25 to £6730 to 40 minutes or more
Xenon or HID bulb£20 to £100High voltage, not a driveway job
LED bulb or module£10 to £150Only legal in a unit built for it
Ford Fiesta, typical£16 to £28Bumper make and model estimates
Volkswagen Golf, typical£18 to £32
BMW 3 Series, typical£16 to £24
Mercedes-Benz C-Class, typical£20 to £32

Set that against the test itself. The legal maximum MOT fee is £54.85 for a car, £58.60 for a class 7 goods vehicle between 3,000kg and 3,500kg, and £29.65 for a standard motorcycle. A bulb fail followed by a paid full retest costs more in retest fee than in parts, which is exactly why the retest rule below is the thing to get right.

The free retest, and the one exception

GOV.UK lists the items that get a free partial retest if you take the vehicle away and bring it back to the same test station before the end of the next working day. The list includes lamps, rear reflectors, electrical wiring, registration plates, the main beam tell-tale, and headlamp cleaning or levelling devices that do not need an aim check.

The wording on the lamps entry is "lamps (excluding headlamp aim)". That exclusion is the whole game. Fix a blown bulb overnight, return the next working day, and the retest is free. Fail on aim and you are into a partial retest fee within ten working days, or a full fee after that. Leaving the vehicle at the station for repair and having it retested within ten working days is free in every case, which for an aim adjustment is often the cheaper route even allowing for the labour. The same logic runs through the guides on brake failure costs and tyre failure costs, where brakes are not on the free list and tyres are.

Vans and motorcycles read differently

For class 7 goods vehicles between 3,000kg and 3,500kg, lamps are worse on every measure: 17.63 percent of the 1,107,819 tests in 2025 to 2026, 30.58 percent of all defects and 34.26 percent of Major defects, against an overall failure rate of 34.00 percent. Roughly one van in six failed something in section 4. Vans that spend their lives reversing into loading bays lose rear lamp units and reversing lamps at a rate cars do not, and end outline marker lamps are mandatory on vehicles first used on or after 1 April 1991 that are wider than 2,100mm, a rule most van owners have never heard of.

Motorcycles invert the picture. On 1,019,745 class 1 and 2 tests, lamps and reflectors were 7.31 percent of tests, lower than cars, but 40.74 percent of all motorcycle defects and 46.62 percent of Major ones. Most strikingly, lamps were 19.43 percent of all Dangerous motorcycle defects against 1.27 percent on a car. The reason is arithmetic: most bikes have one headlamp and one brake light, so a failure that leaves a car with a spare leaves a bike with nothing. Our guide on the motorcycle MOT covers the class 1 and 2 numbers in full.

Reading lamps lines in a used vehicle record

Because lamps are a quarter of all defects, almost every car with a few years of history has one somewhere, which makes the line close to worthless as a signal on its own. Do not discount a car because it once failed on a brake light. Four patterns do carry information.

  • One or two lamp lines across many years. Normal. Ignore it.
  • A headlamp aim fail that repeats across tests or owners. Worth asking about. Aim drifts when the front of the car has been apart, so repeated aim failures can sit alongside accident repair or tired front suspension. Cross-read the suspension lines in the same record.
  • "Light source and lamp not compatible". Someone fitted an LED or HID kit into a halogen unit, and it usually travels with other cheap modifications.
  • Several lamps defects in one test on a recent vehicle. More often a wiring or earth fault than four bulbs failing at once, which is a diagnostic bill rather than a bulb bill.

Every one of those lines sits in the free DVSA record with its manual reference, and you can read the whole trail for any UK registration on the MOT Check UK home page. Advisories are a separate skill, covered in what MOT advisories actually mean.

Plain verdict

Lights are the most common thing wrong with a British vehicle at its MOT and, on a car, one of the least serious: a quarter of all recorded defects and barely one percent of the dangerous ones. If your car fails on a bulb, buy the bulb, fit it or have it fitted for a few pounds, and take the car back to the same station by the end of the next working day so the retest costs nothing. If it fails on aim, ask whether the tester can adjust it, check the dash beam dial is not left high, and consider leaving the car at the station, because aim is the one lamps item the free next day retest does not cover. If you are buying, a lamps line in the history is noise. A repeated aim failure, or a note that the light source and lamp are not compatible, is worth a question.

Figures in this guide: DVSA MOT testing data for Great Britain, initial failures by defect category for classes 1 and 2, 3 and 4, and 7, 2025 to 2026 total and quarterly, published 10 September 2026, and MOT test results by class of vehicle for the same period. DVSA MOT inspection manual for cars and passenger vehicles, section 4, as published on GOV.UK and read on 18 September 2026. GOV.UK pages "Getting an MOT: MOT costs" and "Getting an MOT: retest after a repair". Bumper headlight bulb replacement cost guide, updated 19 September 2025.

title: Motorcycle MOT failure costs in 2026: what a bike fail really costs, and the free retest that excludes bikes
desc: Bikes fail 13.40 percent of MOTs against 27.51 percent for cars and vans. What actually fails a motorcycle, what each repair costs in 2026, and the GOV.UK retest rule that gives cars a free tyre retest but not motorcycles. Free MOT history checks for cars, vans, motorcycles and lorries.
body:
A motorcycle fails its MOT far less often than a car, and when it does fail it is more likely to be for something that could actually hurt the rider. This guide is about what a bike failure costs to put right in 2026. It uses the DVSA figures for classes 1 and 2, and sets them against cars and light vans in classes 3 and 4 where the comparison earns its place. In summary:

  • 13.40 percent of motorcycle MOTs failed first time in the 2025 to 2026 year, against 27.51 percent of cars and light vans. A bike is roughly half as likely to fail.
  • Of the 136,626 bikes that failed first time, 53,012 were repaired at the test station and passed the same day. Nearly two in five failures never left the bay.
  • Lamps and reflectors are 40.74 percent of every motorcycle defect. Tyres are only 8.84 percent, but 34.77 percent of the dangerous ones.
  • The free next working day retest covers lamps on a bike. It expressly does not cover wheels and tyres on a motorcycle, although it does on a car. That one bracket in the GOV.UK list is the most expensive sentence in the rules for riders.
  • The legal maximum test fee is £29.65 for a motorcycle and £37.80 with a sidecar. You can read any UK bike's full test history free at MOT Check UK, which covers cars, vans, motorcycles and lorries.

What actually fails a motorcycle

DVSA publishes initial failures by defect category for every test class. The full 2025 to 2026 year for classes 1 and 2, meaning motorcycles with and without sidecars, was published on 10 September 2026 and covers 1,019,745 tests. This is the whole picture, biggest category first.

Defect categoryPercent of testsPercent of all defectsPercent of Dangerous defects
Lamps and reflectors7.3140.7419.43
Brakes3.1618.2524.77
Structure and attachments2.0811.239.84
Suspension1.9710.203.23
Tyres1.858.8434.77
Steering1.245.846.76
Identification of the vehicle0.923.91none recorded
Wheels0.170.761.20
Audible warning (horn)0.060.24none recorded

Two things jump out. Lamps are four in ten of everything written on a motorcycle ticket, which is more concentrated than on a car, where the same category is 24.89 percent. And tyres, a category most riders assume they have under control, produce a third of all the dangerous defects on British bikes off less than two percent of tests.

This is not a one year pattern. The April to June 2026 quarter came in at 12.40 percent overall, with lamps at 41.89 percent of defects and tyres at 35.03 percent of dangerous ones. The shape holds.

Bikes fail less often, but sharper

The headline comparison flatters motorcycles and then takes some of it back.

Measure, 2025 to 2026Motorcycles, classes 1 and 2Cars and light vans, classes 3 and 4
Initial failure rate13.40 percent27.51 percent
Tests with at least one Dangerous defect4.11 percent7.22 percent
Share of failures carrying a Dangerous defectabout 31 percentabout 26 percent
Average defects per failed test1.772.39
Final failure rate after repairs at the station8.20 percent22.30 percent

A failing bike carries fewer faults than a failing car, which fits the machine: there is less of it, and most of it is visible without taking anything apart. But a bike failure is more likely than a car failure to include something categorised Dangerous, and the gap between the initial 13.40 percent and the final 8.20 percent is the real story of the motorcycle MOT. Of the 136,626 bikes that failed at first inspection, 53,012 were put right at the test station and passed the same day, which DVSA records as a pass after rectification. Only 83,614 bikes in the country were actually sent away failed. On cars the same repair-in-the-bay route closes far less of the gap.

That is worth knowing before you book. A large share of bike failures are a bulb, a plate, a loose chain guard or a horn, and a workshop that tests and repairs under one roof will simply fix them while the bike is on the ramp.

The retest rule that treats bikes differently

There are three retest routes on GOV.UK and the difference between them is worth real money.

  • Leave the bike at the test centre for repair, retested within 10 working days. No fee at all. This is the cheapest route for anything you cannot fix yourself.
  • Take the bike away and bring it back to the same centre before the end of the next working day. Free partial retest, but only on a listed set of items.
  • Take it away and bring it back within 10 working days. A partial retest fee can be charged. Later than that, you pay the full test fee again.

The next working day list is where motorcycles are singled out. It includes lamps but excluding headlamp aim, electrical wiring, registration plates, rear reflectors, mirrors, the horn, seats, and sharp edges or projections. It also includes wheels and tyres, and the entry reads, word for word, "wheels and tyres (excluding motorcycles and motorcycles with sidecar)".

So the biggest failure category on a bike, lamps at 40.74 percent of defects, gets a free next day retest. The category that produces a third of all dangerous motorcycle defects, tyres, does not, even though the rider of a car with the same fault would get one. Brakes are not on the list for any vehicle, and brakes are another 24.77 percent of dangerous bike defects. Add those two and roughly three in five dangerous motorcycle defects sit in categories with no free next day route at all. For those, leaving the bike at the station is usually the cheaper decision, not the lazy one. The equivalent rules for four wheels are in our guides on tyre failure costs and lights failure costs.

What each failure costs to put right in 2026

Published motorcycle repair prices are rare, because most workshops quote by the job. The figures below come from the public price lists of two independent specialists, MD Racing in Walton-on-Thames and Two Tyres in London, read on 19 September 2026. They are one workshop's prices in the south east, not a national average, and your local rate will differ. They are included because they are real and checkable rather than invented.

JobPublished price, September 2026Note
Workshop labour, independent specialist£60 an hour including VATSome main dealers quoted at over £90 an hour plus VAT
Tyre fitting, loose wheels£15 one, £30 a pairIncludes balancing, valves and disposal
Tyre fitting, wheels off the bike£30 one, £60 a pairCruisers and scooters run to about £70 a pair because the exhaust comes off
Front brake pads, one side£36Non-sintered, parts only
Front brake pads, both sides£69.95
Rear brake pads£27.50
Fitting brake pads£26 per caliper30 minutes, includes caliper clean and piston check
Front brake disc£140 to £340 eachFitting £26 per disc
Brake fluid change and bleed£40 front, £20 rear
Front fork rebuild£240 parts and labourSeals, oil, level set
Rear shock rebuild£180 parts and labour

Read that against the defect table and the arithmetic is clear. The most common failure on a British motorcycle is a lamp, which is usually a bulb and a few pounds, and it comes with a free next day retest. The most dangerous common failure is a tyre, which is a tyre plus £15 to £30 of fitting, and it does not. The worst case on the list, a fork rebuild after a suspension or steering fail, is £240, and suspension is only 3.23 percent of dangerous bike defects, so it is rare as well as expensive.

The fee, and when the bike is due

The maximum a station may charge is £29.65 for a motorcycle of any engine size and £37.80 for a motorcycle with a sidecar. Three-wheeled vehicles up to 450kg unladen are £37.80 and over that weight £54.85, the same as a car. There is no VAT on the test fee. A bike needs its first MOT at three years old, the same as a car.

Those numbers matter because they change what a failure is worth arguing about. A car owner facing a second full fee is looking at £54.85. A rider is looking at £29.65, which is less than an hour of workshop labour. If a fault genuinely needs parts ordering, paying a second test fee later is sometimes cheaper than rushing a bodge to beat the next working day deadline.

What to check yourself, and what not to pay for

You do not need to buy a pre-MOT check. For a motorcycle it is close to a waste of money, because the categories that fail most are the ones you can inspect in a well lit garage in ten minutes with no tools. Lamps, reflectors, the registration plate, the horn, chain tension and the general state of the tyres between them account for well over half of all recorded defects.

Two things are worth more than a paid inspection. First, sit on the bike and have someone walk round while you work every light, including the brake light on both levers and the indicators front and rear. Second, look properly at the tyres in daylight rather than in a dark garage, because tread depth rules for bikes are not the car rules and a tyre that looks legal often is not. We set the bike tread rule out in full in the guide on what the DVSA data says really fails a bike.

It is also worth remembering what the test never covers. The MOT says nothing about the engine, the clutch or the gearbox. A bike can pass with a slipping clutch and a rattling top end, so a clean certificate is a roadworthiness statement, not a mechanical one.

Reading a bike's record before you buy

Every failure above stays in the free DVSA record with its category, and the pattern says more than any single line. Four readings are worth having.

  • A lamps failure or two across the years. Ignore it. Four in ten bike defects are lamps, so almost every used machine has one somewhere.
  • A dangerous tyre line. Worth asking about, especially if it repeats. Tyres are only 1.85 percent of tests but a third of dangerous defects, so a bike that has been failed on rubber more than once has usually been ridden to the cords rather than caught early.
  • Structure and attachments defects. This is 11.23 percent of bike defects and it covers frame corrosion, insecure fittings and damaged bodywork. Repeated entries here on an older machine are the closest the record comes to hinting at a hard life or a past accident.
  • A long gap with no test. Normal on a bike and not a red flag on its own, because most machines are laid up over winter and many are declared off the road for years. We set out which gaps matter in why a bike's MOT record has gaps.

Plain verdict

A motorcycle MOT is cheap, it is passed far more often than a car MOT, and about two in five of the failures are put right at the station before the bike leaves. If yours fails on a light, fix it and take it back the next working day, because that retest is free. If it fails on tyres or brakes, do not rush it back: those are the two categories carrying most of the danger, neither gets a free next day retest for a bike, and leaving the machine at the station for repair within ten working days costs nothing at all. Skip the paid pre-MOT inspection and spend ten minutes with the lights and the tyres instead. If you are buying rather than testing, a lamps line means nothing, a repeated dangerous tyre line means something, and repeated structure defects mean you should look very hard at the frame.

Figures in this guide: DVSA MOT testing data for Great Britain, initial failures by defect category for classes 1 and 2 and for classes 3 and 4, and MOT test results by class of vehicle, 2025 to 2026 total and the April to June 2026 quarter, published 10 September 2026.
